Gemini 3.1 Pro matches it with a 1 million input-token window, billed at $2 per million tokens up to 200,000 tokens and $4 per million beyond that threshold [3][4].

Do the arithmetic and a full-context approach looks almost free for a one-off question. Anthropic’s own contextual retrieval write-up makes the same point directly: if your knowledge base is under roughly 200,000 tokens, about 500 pages, you can just paste the whole thing into the prompt and skip retrieval infrastructure entirely, especially once prompt caching absorbs the repeated cost [1]. For a lot of internal tools and single-user assistants, that’s the entire architecture decision settled in one sentence.

Why a longer window doesn’t mean more reliable recall

The part that the window-size marketing leaves out is what happens to accuracy once you actually fill that window. NVIDIA’s RULER benchmark tested models against their advertised context lengths and found that “only half of them can maintain satisfactory performance at the length of 32K,” even though those same models score close to perfect on a simple needle-in-a-haystack retrieval check [5]. Passing the easy version of the test and failing the realistic one is the pattern across the board, not a quirk of one model.

Chroma’s “Context Rot” study pushed on this further by holding task difficulty constant and scaling input length from 25 words up to 10,000, across 18 models including Claude 4, Gemini 2.5, and GPT-4.1 [6]. Performance didn’t degrade in a straight line. It degraded unevenly, worsening faster when a question’s wording didn’t closely match the answer’s wording, and worsening further in the presence of even one distractor sentence. The researchers also found a consistent gap between focused prompts of roughly 300 tokens and full prompts of roughly 113,000 tokens on the same underlying task [6]. I wrote about the mechanics behind this in Context engineering: drift, bloat, and the lost-in-the-middle problem, and the original “Lost in the Middle” research from 2023 is still the clearest explanation for why: models reliably read the start and end of a long input better than the middle of it [7].

Anthropic’s contextual retrieval experiment shows retrieval accuracy is still a solvable, separate problem from window size.

Retrieval sidesteps this by construction. A good retriever hands the model three or four tightly relevant passages instead of three hundred loosely relevant ones, so there’s less haystack for the needle to get lost in. That’s a reliability argument, and it holds even when the budget for context is effectively unlimited.

The real cost of dumping everything into the prompt

Price-per-token tables make long context look cheap, but they hide a multiplier that retrieval avoids: you pay for the context on every single call, not once. A 150,000-token knowledge base re-sent on every user question at Claude Sonnet 5’s uncached input rate costs roughly $0.30 per call before the model has generated a single output token. Anthropic’s own prompt caching brings that down substantially since cached reads price at $0.20 per million tokens instead of $2 [2], but caching has its own constraints around cache lifetime and how often the underlying content changes, which I covered in Prompt caching and token budgeting: what’s documented vs. exam-tested. A knowledge base that updates hourly breaks the cache more often than one that updates monthly, and every cache miss is a full-price re-send.

Retrieval doesn’t eliminate that cost, but it shrinks it to the size of whatever you actually retrieved, which for most queries is a few thousand tokens instead of a few hundred thousand. At scale, the gap compounds: a support bot fielding ten thousand questions a day against a 150,000-token knowledge base is a materially different bill if every call carries the full context versus a few retrieved passages. I laid out a similar per-call-cost lens for choosing between model tiers in Choosing Between Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku: A Cost Framework, and the same logic applies one layer up, to how much context you’re paying to re-process on every single turn.

Both frontier models now advertise a 1M-token window. The pricing structure underneath it is where the real decision lives.

Latency moves in the same direction as cost. A longer input takes longer to process before the model can start generating, even with caching softening the blow on repeat calls. Retrieval keeps the per-call input small and the time-to-first-token short, which matters more than raw throughput for anything a person is sitting in front of waiting for an answer.

Where long context wins outright

None of this makes retrieval the right default everywhere. A full-context approach wins cleanly when the knowledge base is small and static enough to fit comfortably under that 200,000-token threshold Anthropic calls out, when the task genuinely needs to reason across the whole document rather than a slice of it, such as summarizing an entire contract or finding every place a variable is referenced across a codebase, or when the content changes so rarely that a cached context pays for itself across many calls [1][2]. A one-off research assistant reading a single long report, or an internal tool used by five people against a stable 50-page policy document, is exactly the case where building a retrieval pipeline is more engineering than the problem deserves.

A decision framework for 2026

The honest answer, two years after the first wave of RAG hype, is that context window size stopped being the deciding factor. The deciding factors are knowledge base size relative to that 200,000-token caching threshold, how often the content changes, how many calls you’re making against it, and whether the task needs targeted recall or whole-document reasoning. Anthropic’s own data suggests a practical split: under roughly 200,000 tokens of mostly static content, put it all in the prompt and lean on caching; above that, or with content that changes often enough to keep breaking the cache, retrieval earns its complexity back, and contextual retrieval’s reranking layer is worth the extra step once accuracy, not just recall, is what’s being measured [1]. Most systems worth shipping in 2026 end up as a hybrid: a cache-backed full-context pass for the stable core of a knowledge base, with retrieval layered on top for whatever keeps changing underneath it.

The decision tree that replaces “just use the bigger window” as a default.

The context window arms race was never going to make retrieval obsolete, because it was never really solving the problem retrieval solves. A bigger window buys you room. It doesn’t buy you recall, and as RULER, Chroma, and the original “Lost in the Middle” findings all show in their own way, room without reliable recall is just a more expensive way to miss the same chunk [5][6][7].

items.title: Computational tools for society’s most complex challenges
items.summary: As far back as she can remember, Cathy Wu ’12, MNG ’13 wanted to find ways to solve problems to improve people’s lives. Her parents were Taiwanese immigrants, and her father had a long commute to his job, which took him away from the family. On a tight budget, the rest of the family often stayed home on a street that was too busy for playing outdoors. Wu and her siblings ended up playing a lot of computer games. Wu says her desire to make the world a better place, her dad’s daily battle against traffic, and the games she played, like “SimCity,” were the seeds of her motivation to design safe, efficient transportation systems. Wu is an associate professor in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering (CEE) and the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS), and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. Her research focuses on using machine learning and reinforcement learning (RL) to advance reliable strategies for improving a range of complex systems, including transportation. “Designing transportation systems consists of modeling and analyzing dozens, if not hundreds or thousands, of variants, which means that an evidence-driven approach to designing those systems is simply not within reach of today’s tools,” Wu says. “This is the role that RL plays. If successful, it would free transportation researchers and enable their practitioner partners to design the systems they want.” Wu credits her older sister with instilling in her the desire to improve people’s lives, and Wu’s interest in transportation fits neatly into that ideal. “I like transportation because it connects everyone. We all use it, we all experience it, we all have issues with it. So, at some level, we’re all interested in the system being better,” she says. Wu got interested in applying artificial intelligence to transportation while earning her undergraduate degree at MIT, after attending a lecture on autonomous vehicles by the late professor Seth Teller. The lecture, which Teller gave during an Independent Activities Period robotics competition (that Wu actually won), was the event that honed her particular approach to transportation research, Wu says. She began working with Teller, and when he stopped concentrating on autonomous vehicles, he encouraged Wu to transfer to Professor Daniela Rus, who had done research on robotaxis. “I’m very grateful to the people who helped me explore those interests and helped me become the person I am now,” she says, specifically naming Teller, Rus, and “my friends at Dropbox,” who invited her to do a second internship focused on transportation issues. After her master’s degree at MIT, Wu went on to earn her PhD at the University of California at Berkeley. During that time, she observed that transportation researchers were spending years developing optimization methods to model and analyze a single new variant of a system. Her approach as a computer scientist working to develop RL and optimization methodologies to address transportation challenges held the promise of exponentially improved efficiency. In 2018, Wu’s last year of her PhD at UC Berkeley, she successfully applied RL to a traffic problem: automatically analyzing the potential traffic flow impact of autonomous vehicles in a range of different traffic networks. The research went viral. While this could have been a “the rest is history” moment for Wu, RL turned out to be a flighty friend. Wu worked on RL theory in a postdoc at Microsoft and came back to MIT as faculty drawn, she says, by the sustainability focus of CEE, and IDSS’s emphasis on infusing data science into other disciplines. Yet over the next two years, Wu’s further attempts to apply RL to traffic problems failed. “That was stressful,” Wu says, “it was unclear whether the problem was me (the advisor), my students, the traffic domain, or RL itself.” Still, the earlier research was a proof-of-concept demonstration that RL could be applied to transportation systems. And in 2022, she and her students identified that RL algorithms are so sensitive that an algorithm that works on one problem may not on even a closely related one. A key result, which Wu says she is proudest of “because it was like the light at the end of a long tunnel of negative results,” came in 2023. She and her team of researchers devised a way to work around the sensitivity of RL. The team found that while RL may not train well on 90 percent of a group of problems, it can train quite well on 10 percent. And by training RL models on those problems that solve and generalize well, the resultant models collectively perform well on a set of related problems, even those that would not have been solved through direct training. The researchers designed an algorithm to determine which problems to use RL to train, and that algorithm improved training efficiency by up to 30 times, meaning that what would normally have required 100 training models may only require three models. “This work gave me back the confidence that reinforcement learning can play an important role in solving hard optimization problems, including in transportation,” Wu says. “Now, a good chunk of my group works on the topic of contextual RL, which is the setting where RL seeks to solve a space of related problems.” Wu’s more recent research applies RL to solve a hard transportation optimization problem with important policy implications: the work shows that eco-driving measures in which vehicle speeds are intelligently controlled to reduce excessive stopping and starting could reduce vehicle emissions by between 11 and 22 percent. The system provides evidence that policies instituting such measures could significantly improve system efficiency, and is “a demonstration that RL can be used to inform transportation policy on problems of practical importance,” Wu says. “I am a big fan of evidence-based policy and believe it’s the basis for a thriving democratic society, yet our societal systems are so complex,” Wu says. “People can bicker forever about what’s better or worse, but I do believe that there are questions we bicker about that can be analyzed systematically using data and have objective answers. A large part of the reason I am in academia is to better understand how technology can support democratic societal decision-making.” Wu says that much of the work she and her team have done over the last several years has produced algorithms “to streamline the development of solvers for hard optimization problems, whether they are related to transportation or to other systems, such as logistics, supply chains, manufacturing, and resource allocation. “This alludes to my preferred style of work,” Wu says, “which is called use-inspired basic research,” explaining that such research addresses a practical problem, developing fundamental knowledge that often translates to other practical problems. Her students start by probing consequential problems ranging from safety to congestion to accessibility, identifying where existing methods fall short, and allowing the problems themselves to shape the direction of the research. At the same time, Wu’s desire to help others on a more personal level plays out in her teaching. “I love working with students, both in the classroom and research mentoring,” she says. “It makes my day when I am able to teach someone something — when I see that light bulb go on in a student.” In addition to earning academic honors, including a 2023 National Science Foundation Faculty Early Career Development Award, Wu has also been formally celebrated for her teaching and mentoring, including with the Ole Madsen Mentoring Award in 2025. What does she tell students confronting extremely complicated problems? “Be patient. Start small. Societal impact is a lifelong endeavor, not something to be accomplished in a few years,” Wu says. “It will take years to really understand what’s going on and where the real problems are. In the meantime, try to be helpful. Be curious. Ask many questions.”

items.title: How 3 small business owners are — and aren’t — using AI to nail their marketing campaigns
items.summary: From left to right: Small business owners Andrea Garcia Fry, Bonnie Gurry, and Catalina Parker. Courtesy of Natalia Ramos; Nick Starichenko; Maxson Media In August, Meta launched AI tools geared toward small businesses seeking marketing help. Three small business owners shared how they use AI tools for marketing — and their limitations. Testing and organic content remain crucial for small businesses amid the rise of AI marketing tools. Marketing is an integral part of running a small business , but building a successful strategy can be time-consuming for owners. Can AI tools geared toward marketing help? Meta thinks so. In August, it announced new AI features for small business owners, designed to help audit organic Facebook and Instagram posts and ads, measure businesses' performance against similar brands, and offer strategy suggestions to improve marketing efforts. Solo business owners have also tapped generative AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini to assist with time-intensive marketing tasks like customer outreach and content ideation . We asked three small business owners about how they think through and implement marketing strategies in the AI age . The following has been edited for length and clarity. How do AI-assisted tools fit into your overall marketing strategy? Meta announced AI tools for small businesses in August. Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images Andrea Garcia Fry, cofounder at baby and children's clothing brand Arquia: Effective paid media requires an understanding of your brand positioning, tone of voice, business goals, and customer journey. I prefer using ChatGPT or Claude because I can provide fuller context and use them as thought partners. Meta's tool will be valuable if it genuinely learns the business rather than simply recommending more automation or spending. Catalina Parker, founder of the coaching business Relatable Nonprofit: I've tried implementing recommendations directly from Meta Ads Manager, and many of them either didn't work or weren't right for my business. Meta benefits when advertisers spend more money on its platform. I'd rather have a tool that helps me independently analyze the data across my entire marketing ecosystem instead of relying solely on Meta's interpretation of what I should do next. Bonnie Gurry, CEO at climate-friendly investing platform GreenPortfolio: Tools like Meta AI can be great operational time-savers. It's like we now have a junior analyst to run quick diagnostics, spot creative trends, and crank out copy variations in seconds. Similar tools from other ad networks have saved us hours of manual dashboard digging so we can focus on core growth strategy. But you can't let the platform mark its own homework. It's a great assistant for speed, but I wouldn't cede capital allocation or brand positioning decisions to it without validating that its recommendations align with business objectives. What's your biggest challenge when it comes to paid marketing? Paid marketing can quickly become expensive for a small business, said Garcia Fry, the cofounder of baby and children's clothing brand Arquia. Courtesy of Relatable Nonprofit; Arquia; GreenPortfolio Garcia Fry: Paid marketing can become expensive very quickly. Meta needs time and budget to learn who the right customer is, which means a meaningful portion of your investment can be spent during that learning process without producing the results you expected. After that, success isn't guaranteed. Finding the right customer on Meta has been difficult for us, especially with a limited budget. For Arquia, strengthening our brand foundations and organic marketing has brought us better results than our paid campaigns. Parker: Understanding performance across the entire funnel. A lot of people talk about paid ads as the way to scale growth. I learned the hard way that simply putting more money into a campaign because the leads are cheap is not necessarily the answer. You have to track what happens after someone sees the ad. Are they clicking? Opting into the lead magnet? Engaging with your content? Booking a call? Eventually buying? With AI-generated content, bots, and increasing skepticism online, trust feels harder to earn. I'm trying to combine paid acquisition with something much more old-fashioned: consistently nurturing people and building real relationships over time. Gurry: Knowing why an ad worked. Was it the opening hook, the visual, or just a warm retargeting pool? Isolating those creative variables to figure out what actually drove performance, without burning through capital, is a constant balancing act. What is a tool or strategy helping you succeed? Parker uses Instagram to promote her coaching business, Relatable Nonprofit. Courtesy of Maxson Media Garcia Fry: When I run Meta ads, I start with what works organically. If a piece of content resonates with our audience, I may boost it or adapt it into a paid campaign. I also use ChatGPT or Claude to audit the setup, interpret the data, and identify possible tests, but I still make the final decisions. Parker: I've learned not to assume that every recommendation from an expert will work for my business. Testing has been more valuable: knowing which numbers matter, tracking them consistently, testing changes, and using the results to decide what to do next. One of my best-performing campaigns has been running for more than two years with very few changes. It's a simple text-based ad, nothing fancy. It continues to perform despite all the advice about constantly producing new formats. Gurry: We don't need fancy, over-complicated tools. We aim for a clear, back-to-basics look at which ads bring in real clients over time. Quick clicks can burn through a marketing budget with little return on investment if you are not careful. Clicks are great, but not if they aren't reaching your potential customer. And don't outsource strategy to an AI tool — especially one developed by the network that's selling you ads. Read the original article on Business Insider

But you can't let the platform mark its own homework. It's a great assistant for speed, but I wouldn't cede capital allocation or brand positioning decisions to it without validating that its recommendations align with business objectives.

What's your biggest challenge when it comes to paid marketing?Paid marketing can quickly become expensive for a small business, said Garcia Fry, the cofounder of baby and children's clothing brand Arquia.

Courtesy of Relatable Nonprofit; Arquia; GreenPortfolio

Garcia Fry: Paid marketing can become expensive very quickly. Meta needs time and budget to learn who the right customer is, which means a meaningful portion of your investment can be spent during that learning process without producing the results you expected. After that, success isn't guaranteed.

Finding the right customer on Meta has been difficult for us, especially with a limited budget. For Arquia, strengthening our brand foundations and organic marketing has brought us better results than our paid campaigns.

Parker: Understanding performance across the entire funnel. A lot of people talk about paid ads as the way to scale growth. I learned the hard way that simply putting more money into a campaign because the leads are cheap is not necessarily the answer.

You have to track what happens after someone sees the ad. Are they clicking? Opting into the lead magnet? Engaging with your content? Booking a call? Eventually buying?

With AI-generated content, bots, and increasing skepticism online, trust feels harder to earn. I'm trying to combine paid acquisition with something much more old-fashioned: consistently nurturing people and building real relationships over time.

Gurry: Knowing why an ad worked. Was it the opening hook, the visual, or just a warm retargeting pool?

Isolating those creative variables to figure out what actually drove performance, without burning through capital, is a constant balancing act.

What is a tool or strategy helping you succeed?Parker uses Instagram to promote her coaching business, Relatable Nonprofit.

Courtesy of Maxson Media

Garcia Fry: When I run Meta ads, I start with what works organically. If a piece of content resonates with our audience, I may boost it or adapt it into a paid campaign.

I also use ChatGPT or Claude to audit the setup, interpret the data, and identify possible tests, but I still make the final decisions.

Parker: I've learned not to assume that every recommendation from an expert will work for my business. Testing has been more valuable: knowing which numbers matter, tracking them consistently, testing changes, and using the results to decide what to do next.

One of my best-performing campaigns has been running for more than two years with very few changes. It's a simple text-based ad, nothing fancy. It continues to perform despite all the advice about constantly producing new formats.

Gurry: We don't need fancy, over-complicated tools. We aim for a clear, back-to-basics look at which ads bring in real clients over time.

Quick clicks can burn through a marketing budget with little return on investment if you are not careful. Clicks are great, but not if they aren't reaching your potential customer.

And don't outsource strategy to an AI tool — especially one developed by the network that's selling you ads.

items.title: US arrests tech CEO accused of smuggling $300M in Nvidia chips into China
items.summary: The US has arrested another suspect accused of smuggling high-end computer servers containing export-controlled Nvidia chips into China. In a press release on Thursday, the Department of Justice accused 38-year-old Greg Lui of using false paperwork to mask shipments of servers worth more than $300 million that he allegedly knew were ultimately destined for China. As the CEO of Earthmade Computer, Lui allegedly conspired with freight-forwarding firms in South Asian countries like Malaysia and Singapore to illegally divert chip shipments into China, including Nvidia’s A100 GPUs and H100 GPUs, the FBI’s indictment alleged. These are not Nvidia’s most advanced chips. However, the chips can process large amounts of data and train large language models, which the US fears could pose national security risks if China suddenly gets access to enough chips to drastically advance its AI or strengthen its military. Read full article Comments

items.title: Your AI Isn’t Hallucinating. Your Data Is Lying to It.
items.summary: Most of what we call hallucination is a model faithfully repeating data we never checked After years of building enterprise data systems, I have learned that when an AI gives a confidently wrong answer, the first instinct, mine included, is to blame the model. We tune the prompt. We swap in a bigger model. We add another guardrail against “hallucination.” Sometimes that is the right fix. But as production AI moves deeper into retrieval-augmented generation, enterprise search, agents, and workflow automation, I keep finding that a large share of what gets filed under hallucination is not the model inventing anything. It is the model faithfully repeating data that was stale, incomplete, mis-scoped, duplicated, or out of context, data we fed it and never checked. The model is not lying. The data is. This distinction matters because the industry is getting very good at evaluating model behavior while still treating the data layer as somebody else’s plumbing. We measure answer relevance, refusal quality, latency, toxicity, and prompt regressions. But the answer an AI produces is only as reliable as the corpus it retrieves from, the table it queries, the feature view it consumes, and the pipeline that refreshed those assets last night. If those inputs are wrong, the most advanced model in the stack becomes a very fluent messenger for a broken data system. Where bad data and retrieval-layer failures surface as apparent AI hallucinations Two failures wearing one label Hallucination has become the catch-all label for every wrong answer, and that is a problem, because it points every fix at the model. Two very different failures wear the same word. In the first, the model genuinely fabricates, producing something with no basis in what it was given. In the second, the model does its job perfectly and hands back the wrong answer because the input was wrong. Those need opposite fixes, and I keep watching teams apply model-side medicine to a data-side disease. Two failures, one label. The fix lives in a completely different place depending on which one you have. The model did its job Picture a retrieval-augmented assistant answering a customer’s billing question. It retrieves a document, reads it correctly, and answers confidently. The document was superseded three weeks ago, but the job that should have expired it failed silently, so the old version is still in the index. The model did nothing wrong. It grounded its answer in exactly what it was given. What it was given was a lie. Or a summarization agent reporting last quarter’s numbers from a table. A broken upstream join dropped an entire region, so the totals are low. The agent summarizes the table it was handed, accurately, every word faithful to the data. The data is wrong. Call that a hallucination if you like, but no prompt change will fix it. I have watched this exact pattern play out. A team launches an internal AI assistant to help employees answer policy and operations questions. During testing it performs well, because it cites internal documents and gives clear answers. A few months later someone asks about an approval threshold, and the assistant gives the old threshold with full confidence. The answer is not invented. The system retrieved an outdated policy document that stayed in the vector index after the source was replaced. The incident gets reported as a hallucination, so the team starts adjusting prompts and model settings. Only later do they find the real failure: the ingestion pipeline never removed expired content, the index had no document-version awareness, and the answer trace carried no freshness signal. The model was not the root cause. The missing data lifecycle controls were. How to tell which one you actually have The two failures look identical from the outside: a confident wrong answer. But the operating model I rely on separates them in four steps. First, trace the answer back to the exact retrieved source, table, row, field, document version, or tool call. Second, classify whether the answer is unsupported by the evidence or faithfully supported by bad evidence. Third, inspect the source for freshness, scope, lineage, access control, and transformation quality. Fourth, decide where the fix belongs: model behavior, retrieval configuration, data quality, data governance, or upstream engineering. If the model produced a claim that appears nowhere in what it was given, that is fabrication, a model or grounding problem. If the answer faithfully reflects a source that was wrong, stale, or out of scope, then the model behaved correctly and the data failed. That diagnostic discipline sounds basic, but it changes the incident conversation. Instead of writing “the model hallucinated,” teams can write “the answer was unsupported,” “the retrieved policy was expired,” “the index served the wrong business unit,” “the embedding store missed the latest document,” “the structured query used a table with a broken join,” or “the user was allowed to retrieve content outside the intended scope.” Each label points to a different owner and a different remedy. Without that classification, every wrong answer becomes a vague AI problem, and vague AI problems are expensive to fix. The pattern repeats across teams. A spike in “hallucinations” triggers a model swap and a prompt overhaul, and weeks later someone discovers the real cause was a retrieval index still serving documents that expired months ago, or a nightly job that had been failing quietly the whole time. Enormous effort goes into the exciting part, the model, while the boring part that actually broke sits unexamined. The model was never the problem. It was the last honest component in a chain that had gone wrong upstream. Why we blame the model anyway If so many of these are data problems, why does the model take the blame every time? Partly because the model is the visible, exciting part, and reaching for a better one feels like progress. Partly because the data is boring and usually owned by a different team, so “the model hallucinated” is the diagnosis that requires the least uncomfortable conversation. And partly because we can see the model’s output but not the data it consumed at the moment it answered. We debug what is in front of us. The model is in front of us; the stale document buried in a vector index is not. It gets worse as AI starts to act This gets more dangerous as we move from answers to actions. A chatbot that repeats bad data wastes someone’s time. An agent that repeats bad data can act on it: approve the wrong claim, reorder the wrong quantity, route the wrong case, open the wrong ticket, or escalate the wrong customer issue. The confident wrong answer becomes a confident wrong decision, at machine speed, with no human reading every intermediate step. The more autonomy we give these systems, the more the quality of the data they stand on decides the quality of what they do. Agentic AI makes the data problem harder, because the system no longer just retrieves and responds. It plans, calls tools, writes records, updates workflows, and chains decisions across systems. A stale retrieval result can become a bad tool call. A bad tool call can become a downstream operational change. A missing lineage record can make the root cause invisible after the damage is done. In that world, “the model hallucinated” is not a sufficient postmortem. You need end-to-end traces that show what the agent saw, what it retrieved, which data assets it trusted, which tools it called, and which action it took from which source. What to check before you touch the model So before I blame the model, I ask a harder question: was the data it actually saw correct, current, and in scope? Most teams cannot answer that, because they have built elaborate machinery to watch the model, evals, guardrails, prompt versioning, and almost none to watch the data the model consumed. For any wrong answer, make sure you can answer four things: • Grounding: which source did the answer come from, and was that source current, or had it been quietly superseded? • Scope: was the retrieved data something the user behind the request was actually allowed to see? • Distribution: does the data you are feeding the model still look like what it was built on, or has it drifted? • Upstream health: were the jobs and joins that produced this data healthy, or failing silently the whole time? Freshness, scope, distribution, lineage. None of these are model problems, and no amount of prompt engineering touches them. They are unglamorous, which is probably why they get skipped, and they are where a surprising share of “hallucinations” actually live. A practical reliability checklist These are the checks I would make part of the normal AI incident workflow, before anyone reaches for the model: • Log the exact retrieved sources, including document version, table, row, field, timestamp, and access scope. • Capture freshness metadata so an answer can be traced to the age of the content it used. • Monitor retrieval indexes for expired documents, duplicate chunks, missing updates, and stale embeddings. • Validate upstream pipelines for failed jobs, schema drift, broken joins, delayed CDC feeds, and silent data loss. • Separate certified, governed, experimental, and raw datasets so the model does not treat every source as equally trustworthy. • Require provenance for high-impact answers and actions, especially in finance, healthcare, legal, compliance, and customer operations. • Classify every wrong answer as unsupported generation, bad retrieval, bad source data, wrong user scope, or upstream pipeline failure. This is where data observability and AI observability have to meet. Model traces explain how the system responded. Data traces explain whether the system should have trusted what it saw. One without the other leaves a blind spot. The most overhyped fix in AI right now is reaching for a better model to solve a problem that lives in the data. It feels like progress because the model is the exciting part. But AI reliability is not just model reliability. It is retrieval reliability, data reliability, lineage reliability, governance reliability, and operational reliability stitched together. If your AI keeps getting things wrong, stop interrogating the model first and start interrogating what you fed it. In my experience, the model is usually telling the truth about the data. The data is the part that is lying. Your AI Isn’t Hallucinating. items.title: GitHub’s advice for its new Copilot feature is to try something else first
items.summary: GitHub launched computer use in public preview on Thursday , giving Copilot CLI and its desktop app the ability to operate applications on macOS and Windows. Agents can read app content and click, type, scroll, and drag, including in older, GUI-only software with no API, command-line interface, or MCP integration. An expense report in Safari was GitHub’s launch demonstration but the company described other uses including summarizing information in a legacy application, updating a presentation, entering data, and moving information between apps. Developers can access the feature from the terminal or through the Copilot app, which runs on Copilot CLI and launched earlier this year as a rival to Claude Code and Codex . GitHub has some catching up to do. OpenAI added computer use to Codex in April , while Anthropic brought broader computer use on macOS to Claude Code and Claude Cowork earlier this year. GitHub has some catching up to do. Computer use vs. MCP servers Enabling computer use in Copilot CLI activates a bundled plugin with its own MCP server . It works in local sessions, reading application content through the operating system’s accessibility tree and taking screenshots when it needs visual context. The company recommends using direct tools wherever possible. So, if an API, MCP server, terminal command, filesystem tool, or dedicated browser tool can handle the task, it typically provides more structured information and more predictable results than desktop interaction. That advice limits where GitHub thinks computer use belongs. OpenAI president Greg Brockman made a broader case last month , arguing that agents could use the same interfaces as people and spare the industry the work of building and maintaining a connector for every piece of software. Saved approvals outlast their removal Developers enable the feature with /computer on in Copilot CLI or through the Copilot app’s Computer Use settings. macOS also requires Accessibility permission to operate controls and Screen Recording permission to inspect windows when visual context is needed. The CLI session’s permission mode determines whether Copilot asks before accessing an app; developers can check it with /permissions show . When prompted, they can allow access for the current session, choose “Always allow” for future sessions or decline. Deny rules override both automatic and saved approvals. Approvals saved in the CLI carry over to the desktop app on the same computer. Removing an app from the always-allowed list clears its approval for future sessions but leaves access already granted in a running session intact. Stopping work requires a separate action: press Esc twice in the CLI, or click Stop or press Esc in the desktop app. Enterprise controls over computer use Enterprise policy overrides a developer’s local preference. If managed settings block computer use, Copilot CLI reports that the feature is unavailable. Enterprise policy overrides a developer’s local preference. Through managed-settings.json , enterprise owners can also control whether developers may bypass approval prompts . That restriction applies across the Copilot app, CLI, and VS Code. GitHub’s default-enablement policy for Business and Enterprise does not change this preview’s opt-in status. The policy starts applying to unconfigured features on October 22 but excludes preview features. items.summary_html:
GitHub launched computer use in public preview on Thursday, giving Copilot CLI and its desktop app the ability to operate applications on macOS and Windows. Agents can read app content and click, type, scroll, and drag, including in older, GUI-only software with no API, command-line interface, or MCP integration.

An expense report in Safari was GitHub’s launch demonstration but the company described other uses including summarizing information in a legacy application, updating a presentation, entering data, and moving information between apps. Developers can access the feature from the terminal or through the Copilot app, which runs on Copilot CLI and launched earlier this year as a rival to Claude Code and Codex.

GitHub has some catching up to do. OpenAI added computer use to Codex in April, while Anthropic brought broader computer use on macOS to Claude Code and Claude Cowork earlier this year.

GitHub has some catching up to do.

Computer use vs. MCP servers

Enabling computer use in Copilot CLI activates a bundled plugin with its own MCP server. It works in local sessions, reading application content through the operating system’s accessibility tree and taking screenshots when it needs visual context.

The company recommends using direct tools wherever possible. So, if an API, MCP server, terminal command, filesystem tool, or dedicated browser tool can handle the task, it typically provides more structured information and more predictable results than desktop interaction.

That advice limits where GitHub thinks computer use belongs. OpenAI president Greg Brockman made a broader case last month, arguing that agents could use the same interfaces as people and spare the industry the work of building and maintaining a connector for every piece of software.

Saved approvals outlast their removal

Developers enable the feature with /computer on in Copilot CLI or through the Copilot app’s Computer Use settings. macOS also requires Accessibility permission to operate controls and Screen Recording permission to inspect windows when visual context is needed.

The CLI session’s permission mode determines whether Copilot asks before accessing an app; developers can check it with /permissions show. When prompted, they can allow access for the current session, choose “Always allow” for future sessions or decline. Deny rules override both automatic and saved approvals.

Approvals saved in the CLI carry over to the desktop app on the same computer. Removing an app from the always-allowed list clears its approval for future sessions but leaves access already granted in a running session intact.

Stopping work requires a separate action: press Esc twice in the CLI, or click Stop or press Esc in the desktop app.

Enterprise controls over computer use

Enterprise policy overrides a developer’s local preference. If managed settings block computer use, Copilot CLI reports that the feature is unavailable.

Enterprise policy overrides a developer’s local preference.

Through managed-settings.json, enterprise owners can also control whether developers may bypass approval prompts. That restriction applies across the Copilot app, CLI, and VS Code.

GitHub’s default-enablement policy for Business and Enterprise does not change this preview’s opt-in status. The policy starts applying to unconfigured features on October 22 but excludes preview features.

Reliability depends on the interface

A change in timing or window state can cause Copilot to repeat an action or stall. GitHub also warns that the agent may choose the wrong control, type into the wrong field, or struggle with dynamic interfaces and complex workflows.

Sensitive information visible in an application window may also become context for the agent.

Unexpected on-screen content and ambiguous instructions can lead to actions affecting the user’s device, data, or connected accounts. Sensitive information visible in an application window may also become context for the agent.

items.summary: Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out T he Crunchbase Megadeals Board . This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here . This week’s list of the largest U.S. startup funding rounds was pretty much all about AI. That includes the biggest financing — a $1 billion round for Instinct , a developer of AI assistants for everyday tasks — as well as most of the rest of the Top 10. Other large fundraisers include EliseAI , which is deploying AI for the home rental sector, and Armadin , an AI cybersecurity startup. 1. Instinct , $1B, AI assistants: San Francisco-based Instinct, a startup building a personal AI assistant for everyday tasks, secured $1 billion in a Series C round. Sequoia Capital , Benchmark and Coatue backed the financing, which set a $10 billion valuation for the year-old company. 2. EliseAI , $350M, AI for housing: EliseAI, a startup deploying AI for the home rental industry, completed a $350 million funding round at a $4 billion valuation. Andreessen Horowitz and Bessemer Venture Partners led the financing for the New York-based company, which is also expanding into healthcare. 3. Armadin , $255.5M, cybersecurity: Palo Alto, California-based Armadin, an AI-native cybersecurity company focused on autonomous security, raised $255.5 million in Series B funding. Andreessen Horowitz and Accel led the round, which set a valuation of more than $2.5 billion for the year-old startup. 4. Kahua , $250M, project management: Kahua, a platform for enterprises to manage complex capital projects, picked up $250 million in growth funding from Bain Capital Tech Opportunities . The financing set a valuation of over $1 billion for the Alpharetta, Georgia-based company. 5. GMI Cloud , $223M, AI infrastructure: Mountain View, California-based GMI Cloud, a provider of GPU cloud infrastructure used by AI teams to help train and run models, closed on $223 million in Series B funding as well as $445 million in debt financing. Archiv led the round, with participation from Nvidia . 6. General Intuition , $220M, foundational AI: General Intuition,a developer of AI models trained on videos and virtual worlds to develop skills for physical environments, secured $220 million in fresh funding. Valor Equity Partners and Atreides Management were lead backers in the round, which set a $6.2 billion valuation for the New York-based company. 7. (tied) SiMa.ai , $150M, physical AI: SiMa.ai, developer of a software platform for scaling physical AI applications, picked up $150 million in Series C financing at a $1.45 billion valuation. Fidelity and Amplify led the round for the San Jose-based company. 7. (tied) Supabase , $150M, agentic app development: Supabase, provider of an AI-enabled open source Postgres platform for app developers, announced $150 million in new funding led by GIC . The San Francisco-based startup also said it is acquiring database architecture startup Turso . 9. CScale , $145M, AI infrastructure: CScale, a developer of optical interconnect technology for AI data centers, emerged from stealth and says it secured $145 million in Series C funding. Atreides Management , Valor Equity Partners , and Premji Invest led the round for the Palo Alto, California-based startup. 10. Homeward , $120M, real estate: Austin-based Homeward, a startup that helps homeowners buy before selling their existing homes or get cash offers for their properties, closed on $120 million in Series D equity funding led by Saluda Grade . The 8-year-old company also secured $330 million in debt financing. Methodology We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Sept. 26-Oct. 2, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week. Illustration: Dom Guzman

items.title: Cloudflare says its new Clef model means humans no longer need to be in the loop for AI agents
items.summary: With Clef and Clef-flash, Cloudflare is challenging TypeSafe AI's Jev decision model. Clef-flash delivers classifications in about 39 milliseconds, making it more than ten times faster than Jev. Both models are built on Qwen, licensed under Apache 2.0, and designed to let AI agents make structured decisions without generating text. items.title: NVIDIA Announces DGX Spark 64GB: A 1-PetaFLOP Grace Blackwell Desktop for Local AI Agents, Fine-Tuning, and Inference
items.summary: NVIDIA announced a new 64GB configuration of DGX Spark — from Acer, ASUS, Dell, Gigabyte, HP and MSI — its GB10-powered desktop AI system. It gives developers a way to start with one system for local models and agents, then cluster two 64GB units for 128GB of memory across the cluster and more compute when workloads grow. The direct message is: Run open models and always-on agents on your own desk, then cluster DGX Spark system as the work grows – instead of on a metered API. The timing is not accidental. Agents burn tokens continuously through tool calls, retries, long context, and multi-step plans. Token consumption has grown 14x since early 2026. On a cloud API, every one of those tokens is billed. On owned hardware, there is no per-token fee. The 64GB model keeps the same GB10 Grace Blackwell superchip, NVIDIA CUDA accelerated AI software stack, and ConnectX-7 networking as the original — updated with 64GB of unified LPDDR5x instead of 128GB. NVIDIA positions that as enough for today’s most capable 30–35B class open models. NVIDIA continues to offer the 128GB DGX Spark for larger single-box workloads, and clustering 64GB units adds memory and compute together. What is Inside the Box GB10 pairs a Blackwell GPU with 5th-generation Tensor Cores and a 20-core Grace Arm CPU. The GPU delivers up to 1 petaFLOP of FP4 AI compute, with sparsity. Spec DGX Spark 64GB Superchip NVIDIA GB10 Grace Blackwell CPU 20-core Arm (10× Cortex-X925 + 10× Cortex-A725) AI compute Up to 1 petaFLOP FP4 (with sparsity) Memory 64GB LPDDR5x, coherent unified Memory bandwidth 273 GB/s Storage 1, 2, or 4TB NVMe M.2, self-encrypting Networking ConnectX-7 NIC, 200GbE; Wi-Fi 7, BT 5.3 Display 1× HDMI 2.1a OS NVIDIA DGX OS (Ubuntu-based) Size / weight 150 × 150 × 50.5 mm / 1.2 kg Max local model size Up to 100B parameters Availability Oct 23, 2026 — NVIDIA Marketplace, OEM partners, retail Source: NVIDIA specifications. Unified memory is the key design choice: The CPU and GPU share one pool over NVLink-C2C, at 5x the bandwidth of PCIe Gen 5. There is no copying weights between system RAM and VRAM. For agents, that means several models, their KV caches, and tool processes live in one address space. The software is ready on first boot: DGX OS ships with the NVIDIA AI stack, including PyTorch, Jupyter, and Ollama. NVIDIA NemoClaw installs with a single command. It adds privacy and security controls to OpenClaw agents. NVIDIA OpenShell TM , part of the NVIDIA Agent Toolkit TM , adds policy-based guardrails on top. NVIDIA Nemotron TM models are optimized for the box. It runs on a standard wall outlet: No server room, no special cooling. That is important for an agent meant to run around the clock. Built-in networking for clustering: ConnectX-7 lets two DGX Spark 64GB systems cluster for 128GB of memory and more compute. NVIDIA Sync Cluster Assistant simplifies setup. Which Open Models Fit in 64GB Hardware is half the story. The other half is that 30B-class open models got good enough for agent work. Model Developer Type Footprint Role on a Spark Muse Glimmer Meta 29.6B dense, text + image, Apache 2.0 ~17GB (quantized) Main agent model Nemotron 3.5 Lightning NVIDIA 30B MoE (30B-A3B) NVFP4 checkpoint Fast executor for long-running agents Qwen3.8-27B Alibaba Qwen 27B dense ~13.5GB weights (4-bit) General agent and coding Footprints are weight-only estimates; KV cache and runtime overhead come on top. Muse Glimmer is the main model. Meta distilled it from Muse Spark, the model family behind the Meta AI assistant. It targets local agents: reliable tool calls, long multi-step tasks, and recovery from failures. Meta reports 51.2 on SWE-Bench Pro and 75.5 on MCP Atlas. Context runs to 131K tokens. It is also available as an NVIDIA NIM . Full BF16 Glimmer needs 55GB+, which leaves almost nothing for context. The ~17GB quantized build is the practical choice on 64GB. Larger models like DeepSeek V4 Flash need more than one box. NVIDIA’s own benchmarks run it on 4 64 GB clustered Sparks. 5 Things You Can Build on One Box 1. An always-on personal agent Install Hermes and point it at Muse Glimmer or Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. Give it tools: your GitHub repos, a test runner, an RSS feed of arXiv categories. Let it run overnight. By morning it has triaged new issues, reproduced a failing test, and drafted a pull request for review. It has also summarized the 30 papers you would never have opened. Your private notes, code, and email never leave the machine. 2. Fine-tune a coding model on your own repo QLoRA on a 70B model fits in 64GB. Train it on your codebase, internal docs, and past PR reviews. Then serve it locally as a coding assistant that knows your conventions. NVIDIA measured ~18,400 tokens/s on a single node for nanochat distributed fine-tuning. 3. A day-1 model evaluation bench A new open-weight model drops on Hugging Face. Pull it through Ollama or vLLM the same day. Run your own question set against it. Score accuracy, then measure time to first token (TTFT) and tokens per second. Compare it against your current model. There is no API bill for re-running the eval 50 times. 4. A multi-model agent team Unified memory lets several models share one pool. Run Bonsai 2 as a router, and Glimmer as the main reasoning agent. That is roughly 23GB of weights. The rest covers KV cache, the OS, and tool processes. When a problem exceeds local capacity, the agent can send a sanitized question to a larger cloud model. 5. Edge and robotics prototyping Fine-tune a vision transformer for a specific task, like spotting anomalies on a factory floor camera. Validate it locally with the same CUDA stack. Then deploy it to an NVIDIA Jetson device at the edge. When One Box is Not Enough: Clustering with NVIDIA Sync Every DGX Spark ships with ConnectX-7 at 200GbE. Clustering is a native feature, not an add-on. Setup Pooled memory AI compute (FP4) Connection 1 Spark (64GB) 64GB Up to 1 PFLOP — 2 Sparks (64GB each) 128GB Up to 2 PFLOPS Direct QSFP cable, no switch 2 Sparks (128GB each) 256GB Up to 2 PFLOPS Direct QSFP cable, no switch 3 Sparks (128GB each) 384GB Up to 3 PFLOPS QSFP ring, no switch 4 Sparks (128GB each) 512GB Up to 4 PFLOPS 200GbE switch (QSFP56-DD, RoCE v2) Source: NVIDIA. 3-node compute derived from per-unit specs. NVIDIA states 2 clustered 64GB units deliver up to 1.7x the performance of one 128GB DGX Spark. The reason is doubled AI compute and bandwidth: 2 units provide up to 546 GB/s combined, double a single box. NVIDIA Sync is the management layer. The Windows and macOS app discovers Sparks on your network and manages SSH access. Its Cluster Assistant configures ConnectX-7 networking for up to 4 systems. Nodes can also connect across locations over a Tailscale mesh, with no cloud in the data path. The pattern is quite clear. Clustering roughly halves time to first token per doubling and scales fine-tuning near-linearly. Decode improves more modestly, about 1.4x at 4 nodes. For agents that read long inputs, the TTFT gain is the one that matters. Step-by-step multi-node guides, including vLLM on stacked Sparks , are at build.nvidia.com/spark . What It is, and What It is Not Not a chat server for 100 users: 273 GB/s of bandwidth limits concurrent decode throughput. Built for long-input, short-output work: Reading a repo, a log dump, or a paper stack, then writing a short result. 64GB caps one box at 100B parameters: For more, cluster 2 units or choose the 128GB configuration. Key Takeaways DGX Spark 64GB keeps GB10, 1 PFLOP FP4, and the full NVIDIA AI stack. 64GB runs today’s 30–35B class open models, like Qwen 3.8 27B and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. Best uses: always-on agents, QLoRA fine-tuning, and day-1 model evals — no per-token fees. 2 units cluster over ConnectX-7 via NVIDIA Sync for 128GB and up to 1.7x a 128GB Spark. Available October 23; the DGX Spark 128GB remains available. Check out the DGX Spark product page , NVIDIA Sync , and DGX Spark playbooks . Thanks to the NVIDIA team for the thought leadership / resources for this article. This article is sponsored by NVIDIA.
items.summary_html:
NVIDIA announced a new 64GB configuration of DGX Spark — from Acer, ASUS, Dell, Gigabyte, HP and MSI — its GB10-powered desktop AI system. It gives developers a way to start with one system for local models and agents, then cluster two 64GB units for 128GB of memory across the cluster and more compute when workloads grow.

The direct message is: Run open models and always-on agents on your own desk, then cluster DGX Spark system as the work grows – instead of on a metered API.

The timing is not accidental. Agents burn tokens continuously through tool calls, retries, long context, and multi-step plans. Token consumption has grown 14x since early 2026. On a cloud API, every one of those tokens is billed. On owned hardware, there is no per-token fee.

The 64GB model keeps the same GB10 Grace Blackwell superchip, NVIDIA CUDA accelerated AI software stack, and ConnectX-7 networking as the original — updated with 64GB of unified LPDDR5x instead of 128GB. NVIDIA positions that as enough for today’s most capable 30–35B class open models. NVIDIA continues to offer the 128GB DGX Spark for larger single-box workloads, and clustering 64GB units adds memory and compute together.

What is Inside the Box

GB10 pairs a Blackwell GPU with 5th-generation Tensor Cores and a 20-core Grace Arm CPU. The GPU delivers up to 1 petaFLOP of FP4 AI compute, with sparsity.

SpecDGX Spark 64GBSuperchipNVIDIA GB10 Grace BlackwellCPU20-core Arm (10× Cortex-X925 + 10× Cortex-A725)AI computeUp to 1 petaFLOP FP4 (with sparsity)Memory64GB LPDDR5x, coherent unifiedMemory bandwidth273 GB/sStorage1, 2, or 4TB NVMe M.2, self-encryptingNetworkingConnectX-7 NIC, 200GbE; Wi-Fi 7, BT 5.3Display1× HDMI 2.1aOSNVIDIA DGX OS (Ubuntu-based)Size / weight150 × 150 × 50.5 mm / 1.2 kgMax local model sizeUp to 100B parametersAvailabilityOct 23, 2026 — NVIDIA Marketplace, OEM partners, retail

Source: NVIDIA specifications.

Unified memory is the key design choice: The CPU and GPU share one pool over NVLink-C2C, at 5x the bandwidth of PCIe Gen 5. There is no copying weights between system RAM and VRAM. For agents, that means several models, their KV caches, and tool processes live in one address space.

The software is ready on first boot: DGX OS ships with the NVIDIA AI stack, including PyTorch, Jupyter, and Ollama. NVIDIA NemoClaw installs with a single command. It adds privacy and security controls to OpenClaw agents. NVIDIA OpenShellTM, part of the NVIDIA Agent ToolkitTM, adds policy-based guardrails on top. NVIDIA NemotronTM models are optimized for the box.

It runs on a standard wall outlet: No server room, no special cooling. That is important for an agent meant to run around the clock.

Built-in networking for clustering: ConnectX-7 lets two DGX Spark 64GB systems cluster for 128GB of memory and more compute. NVIDIA Sync Cluster Assistant simplifies setup.

Which Open Models Fit in 64GB

Hardware is half the story. The other half is that 30B-class open models got good enough for agent work.

ModelDeveloperTypeFootprintRole on a SparkMuse GlimmerMeta29.6B dense, text + image, Apache 2.0~17GB (quantized)Main agent modelNemotron 3.5 LightningNVIDIA30B MoE (30B-A3B)NVFP4 checkpointFast executor for long-running agentsQwen3.8-27BAlibaba Qwen27B dense~13.5GB weights (4-bit)General agent and coding

Footprints are weight-only estimates; KV cache and runtime overhead come on top.

Muse Glimmer is the main model. Meta distilled it from Muse Spark, the model family behind the Meta AI assistant. It targets local agents: reliable tool calls, long multi-step tasks, and recovery from failures. Meta reports 51.2 on SWE-Bench Pro and 75.5 on MCP Atlas. Context runs to 131K tokens. It is also available as an NVIDIA NIM.

Full BF16 Glimmer needs 55GB+, which leaves almost nothing for context. The ~17GB quantized build is the practical choice on 64GB.

Larger models like DeepSeek V4 Flash need more than one box. NVIDIA’s own benchmarks run it on 4 64 GB clustered Sparks.

5 Things You Can Build on One Box 1. An always-on personal agent

Install Hermes and point it at Muse Glimmer or Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. Give it tools: your GitHub repos, a test runner, an RSS feed of arXiv categories. Let it run overnight.

By morning it has triaged new issues, reproduced a failing test, and drafted a pull request for review. It has also summarized the 30 papers you would never have opened. Your private notes, code, and email never leave the machine.

2. Fine-tune a coding model on your own repo

QLoRA on a 70B model fits in 64GB. Train it on your codebase, internal docs, and past PR reviews. Then serve it locally as a coding assistant that knows your conventions.

NVIDIA measured ~18,400 tokens/s on a single node for nanochat distributed fine-tuning. 

3. A day-1 model evaluation bench

A new open-weight model drops on Hugging Face. Pull it through Ollama or vLLM the same day. Run your own question set against it.

Score accuracy, then measure time to first token (TTFT) and tokens per second. Compare it against your current model. There is no API bill for re-running the eval 50 times.

4. A multi-model agent team

Unified memory lets several models share one pool. Run Bonsai 2 as a router, and Glimmer as the main reasoning agent. That is roughly 23GB of weights.

The rest covers KV cache, the OS, and tool processes. When a problem exceeds local capacity, the agent can send a sanitized question to a larger cloud model.

5. Edge and robotics prototyping

Fine-tune a vision transformer for a specific task, like spotting anomalies on a factory floor camera. Validate it locally with the same CUDA stack. Then deploy it to an NVIDIA Jetson device at the edge.

When One Box is Not Enough: Clustering with NVIDIA Sync

Every DGX Spark ships with ConnectX-7 at 200GbE. Clustering is a native feature, not an add-on.

SetupPooled memoryAI compute (FP4)Connection1 Spark (64GB)64GBUp to 1 PFLOP—2 Sparks (64GB each)128GBUp to 2 PFLOPSDirect QSFP cable, no switch2 Sparks (128GB each)256GBUp to 2 PFLOPSDirect QSFP cable, no switch3 Sparks (128GB each)384GBUp to 3 PFLOPSQSFP ring, no switch4 Sparks (128GB each)512GBUp to 4 PFLOPS200GbE switch (QSFP56-DD, RoCE v2)

Source: NVIDIA. 3-node compute derived from per-unit specs.

NVIDIA states 2 clustered 64GB units deliver up to 1.7x the performance of one 128GB DGX Spark. The reason is doubled AI compute and bandwidth: 2 units provide up to 546 GB/s combined, double a single box.

NVIDIA Sync is the management layer. The Windows and macOS app discovers Sparks on your network and manages SSH access. Its Cluster Assistant configures ConnectX-7 networking for up to 4 systems. Nodes can also connect across locations over a Tailscale mesh, with no cloud in the data path.

The pattern is quite clear. Clustering roughly halves time to first token per doubling and scales fine-tuning near-linearly. Decode improves more modestly, about 1.4x at 4 nodes. For agents that read long inputs, the TTFT gain is the one that matters.

Step-by-step multi-node guides, including vLLM on stacked Sparks, are at build.nvidia.com/spark.

What It is, and What It is Not
  • Not a chat server for 100 users: 273 GB/s of bandwidth limits concurrent decode throughput.
  • Built for long-input, short-output work: Reading a repo, a log dump, or a paper stack, then writing a short result.
  • 64GB caps one box at 100B parameters: For more, cluster 2 units or choose the 128GB configuration.
Key Takeaways
  • DGX Spark 64GB keeps GB10, 1 PFLOP FP4, and the full NVIDIA AI stack.
  • 64GB runs today’s 30–35B class open models, like Qwen 3.8 27B and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning.
  • Best uses: always-on agents, QLoRA fine-tuning, and day-1 model evals — no per-token fees.
  • 2 units cluster over ConnectX-7 via NVIDIA Sync for 128GB and up to 1.7x a 128GB Spark.
  • Available October 23; the DGX Spark 128GB remains available.

Check out the DGX Spark product page, NVIDIA Sync, and DGX Spark playbooks.

items.title: Trump Was Reportedly Pushed Into Invading Venezuela by Conversation With Grok
items.summary: It’s hardly a secret that president Donald Trump is addicted to AI slop , but his proclivity for being wooed by the tech apparently doesn’t end there. Trump is also, according to new reporting from TIME magazine, absolutely enthralled by Elon Musk’s Grok chatbot. Whereas your average user might turn to the infamously foul-mouthed AI — which briefly identified itself as “MechaHitler” — to win an online argument or crank out gooning material, the commander in chief uses it for more productive activities such as consulting on his military and geopolitical schemes. An illustrative moment came in December 2025, when Elon Musk returned to the Oval Office for a secret meeting, according to TIME . Trump spent hours asking Grok questions about his presidency and legacy, an official present told the magazine. On the top of Trump’s mind was Venezuela and “narcoterrorism,” supposed threats to the nation that he was combatting by bombing random Venezuelan fishing boats . Trump asked Grok how Venezuelans would react if the US captured the country’s president Nicolas Maduro. And Grok, in classic AI sycophantic fashion, told him what he wanted to hear. The chatbot asserted that Maduro was a deeply unpopular dictator, so Venezuelans would celebrate his ousting. Trump, as you may well know, then went ahead and ordered the technically-not-an-invasion of Venezuela, in a series of military strikes that killed dozens of Venezuelan and Cuban military personnel and several civilians, and led to the capture of Maduro. When news footage showed celebrations in the streets, Trump, officials said, came away convinced that Grok was ingenious. Even setting aside his public love of AI slop, it’s not surprising to hear that Trump’s bewitched by a chatbot. He’s old, for one. And more importantly, he’s someone who surrounds himself with yes-men in real life. An AI chatbot will confirm what he already believes and entertain his whims without any of the friction that may arise with human sycophants such as what happened with his First Buddy, or the numerous appointees he fell out with during his first term . He also, if not outright senile , is visibly showing a diminished mental acuity befitting his years. When TIME interviewed Trump, he struggled to string even two short sentences together in a coherent fashion, such as when he was asked if he liked Sam Altman. “I like him. Do I trust him? Who do I trust? I like Sam Altman,” Trump babbled. “Smart. Dario’s smart. They’re all smart. We’re dealing with a very high level of IQ. Very very high level. That’s a good thing. I like that. I like it. Did you see the story about my uncle?” Trump’s affinity for Grok’s advice isn’t the only incident that calls into question the Trump administration’s embrace of AI in high-level decision-making. The Pentagon has used Grok and Anthropic’s Claude AI to select targets to be bombed in Iran . An AI-targeting system was also used in the February 28th air strikes on the Shajareh Tayyebeh girls’ school that killed over 150 people, including at least 123 children. More on AI: Trump Launched an America.org “Super Intelligence” Chatbot and It Immediately Disagrees With Him on Huge Topics, Including Whether He Won the 2020 Election

items.title: Who is Shivon Zilis? Meet the Elon Musk exec who said their relationship suddenly ended
items.summary: Elon Musk and Shivon Zilis with their twins. Courtesy of Walter Isaacson AI investor and developer Shivon Zilis is a longtime executive at Elon Musk's companies. She said on X that her relationship with Musk went "from in love to let go." A director at Neuralink, Zilis is a plaintiff in the trial and has four children with Musk. Shivon Zilis — a longtime executive at Elon Musk's companies and the mother of four of his children — said her relationship with the billionaire ended "in a week with no warning." In a post on X, Zilis shared a rare glimpse into Musk's romantic life. "I feel happy that I got to show Elon how it feels to be deeply understood, nurtured, and peacefully loved with stability and gentleness," she wrote on Friday. "My heart is full knowing I got to do that, and I hope it leaves a lasting good effect." Zilis and her employer, the Musk-owned Neuralink , didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Musk also didn't respond. She joined Musk at OpenAI in 2016, a year after its founding, and helped helm the company during Musk's investment and his rancorous 2018 split with CEO Sam Altman. From there, Zilis followed Musk to Tesla and his rival project, xAI. She's now the director of operations and special projects at another of the billionaire's companies — Neuralink , a startup that makes computer chips designed to be implanted in the brain. Zilis is also the mother to four of Musk's children. Elon Musk's biographer, Walter Isaacson, shared a glimpse into Musk's relationship with Zilis in September 2023. In an excerpt from Isaacson's biography of the Tesla CEO and in a post on social media, he shared a photo of Musk and Zilis with their twins — who were 16 months old at the time — sitting on each of their laps. Walter Isaacson posted a photo of Elon Musk and Zilis on X. Walter Isaacson on X The biographer said the photo was taken when Musk ushered him to Zilis' house in Austin to talk about the threat AI posed to civilization. "We were sitting on a suburban patio by a tranquil backyard swimming pool on a sunny spring day, with two bright-eyed twins learning to toddle, as Musk somberly speculated about the window of opportunity for building a sustainable human colony on Mars before an AI apocalypse destroyed earthly civilization," Isaacson said of the scene. Here is more you need to know about Zilis: Zilis grew up in Ontario, Canada, and is a lifelong athlete Zilis was born in Markham, Ontario, and grew up playing ice hockey. She attended Yale University, where she played goalie on the women's ice hockey team. She graduated in 2008 with a degree in economics and philosophy. Photos from Zilis' social media accounts, which were taken down in 2022, show Zilis surfing, zip-lining, and ice climbing. She started her career in finance and venture capital After graduating from Yale, Zilis got a job at IBM, where she spent three years focused on financial technologies. She later joined early-stage venture capital fund Bloomberg Beta, where she led investment efforts in data and machine learning. Her work at Bloomberg Beta earned her a spot on Forbes' 30 Under 30 list in the venture-capital category in 2015. Tesla owners broke down the perks of owning a Tesla in conversations with Insider. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Zilis worked as a project director at Tesla from 2017 to 2019, contributing her AI expertise to the Autopilot and chip design teams. She's passionate about artificial intelligence Zilis developed an interest in artificial intelligence around the age of 12 or 13, when she learned about the concept from the Our Lady Peace album "Spiritual Machines." It led her to read a Ray Kurzweil book by a similar name and sparked her passion for AI, she said during a 2021 address at the Canadian Undergraduate Conference on AI . "I've basically spent pretty much all of the last decade focused in and around AI unfolding in the world in the best way possible," she said. It was AI that led her to Musk: In 2016, Zilis joined OpenAI, a nonprofit co-founded by a group that included Musk and former Y Combinator president Sam Altman. OpenAI's stated mission is to find ways for AI to benefit humanity as a whole. The company made headlines when it released a new version of its AI chatbot, ChatGPT in 2023 . Zilis and Musk share a love for fantasy and gaming Like Musk, Zilis appears to have a passion for fantasy and games in the genre. The Neuralink executive posted on X in May that "the fact that a visually rich and dynamic world can live and come alive on a laptop is insane." "We're so normalized to the magic of gaming," Zilis said in the post. "But, when you step back and think about it, it's absolutely wild." She also posted a photo on X in July of talismans from Elden Ring, a fantasy video game set in a world of dungeons and warriors, known for its challenging gameplay. The game is written by "A Song of Fire and Ice" author George RR Martin and produced by FromSoftware, the creators of Dark Souls. The talismans in the game have various powers, such as increasing bow range or stamina recovery. Zilis followed up with a response to the post and said the items were "not religious or witchcraft items." She also added that they have "resonance" for her in the game, "but also to keep in mind as priorities for real life (whether literally or through analogy)." Musk also enjoys playing Elden Ring — to the point where he's reportedly stayed up till 5:30 a.m. playing it. She has a high-level role at Neuralink In 2017, Zilis joined Neuralink, the futuristic brain microchip company also cofounded by Musk. Neuralink has a short-term goal of using implantable devices to solve brain and spine problems, and a long-term mission of achieving "symbiosis" between artificial intelligence and the human brain, according to Musk . Zilis is a director at Neuralink. Photo illustration by Jonathan Raa/NurPhoto via Getty Images In her presentation at the Canadian Undergraduate Conference on AI in 2021, Zilis called Neuralink the most "complicated but also fascinating thing I've ever encountered in my life." "AI's going to be one of the fundamentally transformative technologies humanity creates, if not the most," she said. "And so we just need to make sure, from a humanity perspective, this goes well." In January, Noland Arbaugh became the first human patient to receive a Neuralink brain implant. Zilis has defended Musk from critics In 2020, Musk publicly sparred with the state of California over its COVID-19 lockdown restrictions, calling them "fascist" and "forcible imprisoning." He pledged that Tesla's headquarters would relocate to Texas as a result, prompting California State Assembly member Lorena Gonzalez Fletcher to tweet, "F*ck Elon Musk." Zilis responded on Twitter, writing that Gonzalez Fletcher's tweet made her sad. "No one's perfect but I've never met anyone who goes through more personal pain to fight for an inspiring future for humanity - and has done so tirelessly for decades," Zilis wrote. "Everyone's entitled to their opinion but mine is that there's no one I respect and admire more." This year, she testified at Musk's civil trial against OpenAI's Sam Altman. The trial centered on Musk's claims that Altman took his $38 million early investment in the company behind ChatGPT, then reneged on his promise that it would remain solely nonprofit. Zillis, who joined Musk as a plaintiff in the $134 billion lawsuit that led to the trial, was a key witness , having had a front-row seat to many of the events before the six-member jury. Zilis had twins with Musk in 2021 and bought a house in Austin Business Insider was the first to report that Zilis had twins with the Tesla CEO , who were born in 2021. In 2022, Zilis and Musk filed a petition to change the twins' names in order to "have their father's last name and contain their mother's last name as part of their middle name," according to court documents obtained by Business Insider. Zilis purchased a home in a gated community in Austin in August 2021. Tesla's Gigafactory is located near Austin, and court documents obtained by Business Insider list Musk and Zilis as residents of that address. Musk, however, has said that his primary residence is a $50,000 Tesla tiny house in Boca Chica, near the SpaceX launch facility in South Texas. She is one of several women who have children with Musk There are eight other known living children of Musk aside from those fathered with Zilis: Five are with Musk's first wife , Justine Wilson, and three are with Musk's former girlfriend, the musician Grimes. The billionaire has said in the past that he's doing his best to help the " underpopulation crisis ." Zilis and Musk's twins were born a few weeks before Musk and Grimes had their second child via surrogate. Musk and Grimes later had a third child in June 2022, according to a 2023 biography of Musk.
