items.title: RNNs Explained: How Neural Networks Understand Sequential Data
items.summary: CNNs learned to look at images. RNNs learn to read, listen and follow along. Introduction In the last article, CNNs showed us how a network can understand where things are in an image. But some data isn’t about space at all. It’s about order . Read this sentence backwards and it stops making sense. Shuffle a week of stock prices and the trend disappears. CNNs learn spatial patterns in images. RNNs are designed for information where the order matters. That kind of data is called sequential data , and it’s everywhere: • Sentences and text • Time series and stock prices • Speech and audio • Sensor data • Weather measurements The network built for it is the Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) . Let’s see how it works. What is sequential data? Sequential data is information that comes in a specific order, where each item depends on what came before it. Take a simple sentence: Same words, different order, different meaning. The individual words are identical in both rows. What changed is the order, and with it, everything. An RNN is built around this idea: it processes information one step at a time, while carrying along what it has learned from earlier steps . Why regular neural networks struggle with sequences A traditional neural network, like the ones from our earlier articles, has some awkward limits when it comes to sequences: • It treats each input independently. Once one input is processed, it’s forgotten. • It has no built-in memory of previous inputs. • It expects a fixed input size, but sentences and recordings come in all lengths. Earlier information often matters for understanding what’s happening now. To fill the blank, the model has to remember something said much earlier. “I speak fluent ___” is almost impossible to complete without knowing the speaker grew up in France. We need a network that can remember . What is an RNN? An RNN is a neural network designed to process sequential data by carrying information from previous time steps to the current step. The trick is a loop. At every step the network takes in the new input and also its own hidden state from the previous step, a compact summary of everything it has seen so far. Then it updates that hidden state and passes it on. On the left, the RNN with its loop. On the right, the same thing “unrolled” across time. The idea of memory This is the concept to hold on to. At each step: Current input plus previous memory produces new memory. The hidden state acts as a running summary of the information from previous steps. Think of reading a book and keeping a short note in your head: “so far, the detective suspects the butler.” With each new page you update that note rather than re-reading the whole book. The hidden state is that note. RNN architecture An RNN has three main pieces: the input xₜ at time step t, the hidden state hₜ, and (optionally) an output yₜ. Here’s how one step works: One RNN step: mix the new input with the old memory, squash it, and pass it on. hₜ = f( Wx · xₜ + Wh · hₜ₋₁ + b ) • xₜ: the current input • hₜ₋₁: the previous memory • hₜ: the new, updated memory • Wx, Wh: learnable weights (one set for the input, one for the memory) • b: the bias • f: an activation function, usually tanh Let’s run it with tiny numbers. Let Wx = 0.5, Wh = 0.8, b = 0 and start with h₀ = 0. Feed in the sequence 1, 2, 3: h₁ = tanh(0.5×1 + 0.8×0 ) = tanh(0.50) = 0.462 h₂ = tanh(0.5×2 + 0.8×0.462 ) = tanh(1.37) = 0.879 h₃ = tanh(0.5×3 + 0.8×0.879 ) = tanh(2.20) = 0.976 Notice that h₂ is not just a function of the input 2. It also carries a trace of the earlier input 1. That’s memory in action, in three lines of arithmetic. Unrolling an RNN through time An RNN isn’t really a long chain of different networks. It’s one network applied again and again. Unrolling just lets us draw each time step separately: Four time steps, one set of weights. The weights are shared across time steps. That sharing is important for two reasons. It keeps the parameter count small, and it lets the same RNN handle sequences of any length, because we just repeat the step as many times as we need. How does an RNN learn? What is BPTT? Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) is the method used to train an RNN by propagating errors backward through its sequence of time steps. the end is traced back through every step that contributed to it. Because h₄ depends on h₃, which depends on h₂, which depends on h₁, an error at the end of the sequence traces back through all of them. It’s exactly the chain rule from Article #3, stretched along the time axis. And since the weights are shared, the gradients from all the time steps are added together to update the same weights. Different types of RNN applications Depending on the task, the inputs and outputs can be arranged in a few different ways: Blue circles are inputs, squares are RNN steps, green circles are outputs. • One-to-one: a single input, a single output. This is a plain neural network. • One-to-many: one input produces a sequence. Example: image → caption. • Many-to-one: a sequence produces one output. Example: text → sentiment. • Many-to-many: a sequence in, a sequence out. Example: machine translation. Example: sentiment analysis Take the sentence “The movie was absolutely amazing.” The RNN reads it one word at a time, updating its memory after each word. Only at the end does it produce a verdict: A many-to-one RNN reads the whole sentence before deciding. Each word nudges the hidden state. “absolutely” intensifies whatever comes next, and “amazing” tips the balance. By the final step the hidden state holds a summary of the whole sentence, and that summary is what produces “Positive.” Example: next-word prediction Now a many-to-many setup. After every word, the RNN predicts what comes next. Given “I am learning”, the most likely next word might be “deep”. Then given “I am learning deep”, the natural next word is “learning”. The previous words provide the context that makes the prediction sensible. This is also the basic idea behind language models. The problem with long-term dependencies Basic RNNs have one famous weakness. Consider: “I grew up in India. … [many words later] … I speak fluent ___.” The clue is far back in the sequence. A short-term dependency is when the relevant information is only a few steps away (easy for an RNN). A long-term dependency is when it’s many steps away, and that’s where basic RNNs struggle. The memory gets overwritten a little at every step, and the faint trace of an early word can be gone by the time we need it. Vanishing gradients The reason is mathematical, and it shows up during BPTT. To send the error back through ten time steps, the gradient is multiplied by a factor at every step. The earliest time steps get almost no learning signal, so the network can’t learn to connect them to the outcome. Exploding gradients The opposite can happen too. If the repeated factor is larger than 1, the gradient grows instead: Gradient → × large → × large → × large → … → huge With a factor of 2 per step, ten steps back gives ²¹⁰ = 1,024 times the original gradient. That leads to unstable training, enormous weight updates, and sometimes a loss that turns into NaN. A common fix is gradient clipping : if the gradient gets bigger than a chosen threshold, scale it down before applying the update. Vanishing gradients are harder to fix, which is what motivated the LSTM in the next article. Limitations of RNNs • Difficulty with long-term memory. • Vanishing gradients. • Exploding gradients. • Sequential computation can be slow, since step 5 must wait for step 4. Hard to parallelize across time steps. A simple Python example Let’s teach a tiny RNN to continue a pattern: given [10, 20, 30, 40], predict 50. We’ll train on many sequences that climb by a constant step, but deliberately leave out the exact [10, 20, 30, 40] one so we can test on it. import numpy as np import tensorflow as tf from tensorflow.keras import layers, models, optimizers # 1) Build training data: 4 numbers in, the next number out X, y = [], [] for start in range(1, 21): for step in range(1, 11): if (start, step) == (10, 10): # held out for testing continue seq = [start + step * i for i in range(4)] X.append(seq) y.append(start + step * 4) # Shape must be (samples, time steps, features); scale to small values X = np.array(X, dtype=”float32")[…, None] / 100.0 y = np.array(y, dtype=”float32") / 100.0 # 2) Create the RNN model = models.Sequential([ layers.Input(shape=(4, 1)), layers.SimpleRNN(16), # the recurrent layer with 16 hidden units layers.Dense(1), # turns the final hidden state into a number ]) model.compile(optimizer=optimizers.Adam(0.01), loss=”mse”) # 3) Train model.fit(X, y, epochs=300, batch_size=32, verbose=0) # 4) Predict on the unseen sequence test = np.array([[10, 20, 30, 40]], dtype=”float32")[…, None] / 100.0 print(model.predict(test)[0, 0] * 100) # should be close to 50 A few details worth understanding. The data shape (samples, time steps, features) is how Keras expects sequences. The SimpleRNN(16) layer has 16 × 1 input weights, 16 × 16 recurrent weights and 16 biases, which is 288 parameters in total. And scaling the numbers down matters, because large raw values push tanh into its flat regions where learning stalls. The prediction should land close to 50 but won’t be exactly 50. If it’s well off, train for more epochs. Want to see clipping? Change the optimizer to optimizers.Adam(0.01, clipnorm=1.0). Where are RNNs used? • Speech recognition • Sentiment analysis • Text generation • Time-series forecasting • Language modeling • Sequence classification • Machine translation A note on the present day: because of the limits above, many modern systems use LSTMs, GRUs and Transformers instead of basic RNNs, especially where long-range memory matters. Basic RNNs are still the best place to learn the core idea. Common beginner questions What is the hidden state? A vector of numbers that summarizes everything the network has seen so far in the sequence. Is hidden state the same as memory? Roughly, yes, as an analogy. But it’s a compressed, constantly overwritten summary, not a filing cabinet of exact past inputs. Why are RNN weights shared? So the same learned rule applies at every time step. It keeps the model small and lets it handle sequences of any length. What is BPTT? Backpropagation applied to the unrolled network, sending the error back through each time step. Why do RNNs have vanishing gradients? Because the gradient is multiplied by similar factors at every step going back, and repeated multiplication by numbers below 1 shrinks it toward zero. Can RNNs remember everything? No. Basic RNNs mostly remember recent information well and distant information poorly. RNN vs CNN? CNNs find local patterns in grids like images. RNNs process ordered sequences with a running memory. RNN vs LSTM? An LSTM is an RNN with extra machinery (gates) that decides what to keep, forget and output, which helps it remember over long distances. Conclusion RNNs introduced the idea of giving neural networks a form of memory, allowing them to process information where sequence and order matter. But basic RNNs struggle to hold on to information over long sequences. So how could we build a network that can decide what to remember, what to forget, and what to use? items.summary_html:
CNNs learned to look at images. RNNs learn to read, listen and follow along.Introduction

In the last article, CNNs showed us how a network can understand where things are in an image. But some data isn’t about space at all. It’s about order. Read this sentence backwards and it stops making sense. Shuffle a week of stock prices and the trend disappears.

CNNs learn spatial patterns in images. RNNs are designed for information where the order matters.

That kind of data is called sequential data, and it’s everywhere:

• Sentences and text

• Time series and stock prices

• Speech and audio

• Sensor data

• Weather measurements

The network built for it is the Recurrent Neural Network (RNN). Let’s see how it works.

What is sequential data?

Sequential data is information that comes in a specific order, where each item depends on what came before it. Take a simple sentence:

Same words, different order, different meaning.

The individual words are identical in both rows. What changed is the order, and with it, everything. An RNN is built around this idea: it processes information one step at a time, while carrying along what it has learned from earlier steps.

Why regular neural networks struggle with sequences

A traditional neural network, like the ones from our earlier articles, has some awkward limits when it comes to sequences:

• It treats each input independently. Once one input is processed, it’s forgotten.

• It has no built-in memory of previous inputs.

• It expects a fixed input size, but sentences and recordings come in all lengths.

  • Earlier information often matters for understanding what’s happening now.
To fill the blank, the model has to remember something said much earlier.

“I speak fluent ___” is almost impossible to complete without knowing the speaker grew up in France. We need a network that can remember.

What is an RNN?

An RNN is a neural network designed to process sequential data by carrying information from previous time steps to the current step.

The trick is a loop. At every step the network takes in the new input and also its own hidden state from the previous step, a compact summary of everything it has seen so far. Then it updates that hidden state and passes it on.

On the left, the RNN with its loop. On the right, the same thing “unrolled” across time.The idea of memory

This is the concept to hold on to. At each step:

Current input plus previous memory produces new memory.

The hidden state acts as a running summary of the information from previous steps.

Think of reading a book and keeping a short note in your head: “so far, the detective suspects the butler.” With each new page you update that note rather than re-reading the whole book. The hidden state is that note.

RNN architecture

An RNN has three main pieces: the input xₜ at time step t, the hidden state hₜ, and (optionally) an output yₜ. Here’s how one step works:

One RNN step: mix the new input with the old memory, squash it, and pass it on.

hₜ = f( Wx · xₜ + Wh · hₜ₋₁ + b )

• xₜ: the current input

• hₜ₋₁: the previous memory

• hₜ: the new, updated memory

• Wx, Wh: learnable weights (one set for the input, one for the memory)

• b: the bias

• f: an activation function, usually tanh

Let’s run it with tiny numbers. Let Wx = 0.5, Wh = 0.8, b = 0 and start with h₀ = 0. Feed in the sequence 1, 2, 3:

h₁ = tanh(0.5×1 + 0.8×0 ) = tanh(0.50) = 0.462

h₂ = tanh(0.5×2 + 0.8×0.462 ) = tanh(1.37) = 0.879

h₃ = tanh(0.5×3 + 0.8×0.879 ) = tanh(2.20) = 0.976

Notice that h₂ is not just a function of the input 2. It also carries a trace of the earlier input 1. That’s memory in action, in three lines of arithmetic.

Unrolling an RNN through time

An RNN isn’t really a long chain of different networks. It’s one network applied again and again. Unrolling just lets us draw each time step separately:

Four time steps, one set of weights.

The weights are shared across time steps.

That sharing is important for two reasons. It keeps the parameter count small, and it lets the same RNN handle sequences of any length, because we just repeat the step as many times as we need.

How does an RNN learn?What is BPTT?

Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) is the method used to train an RNN by propagating errors backward through its sequence of time steps.

the end is traced back through every step that contributed to it.

Because h₄ depends on h₃, which depends on h₂, which depends on h₁, an error at the end of the sequence traces back through all of them. It’s exactly the chain rule from Article #3, stretched along the time axis. And since the weights are shared, the gradients from all the time steps are added together to update the same weights.

Different types of RNN applications

Depending on the task, the inputs and outputs can be arranged in a few different ways:

Blue circles are inputs, squares are RNN steps, green circles are outputs.

• One-to-one: a single input, a single output. This is a plain neural network.

• One-to-many: one input produces a sequence. Example: image → caption.

• Many-to-one: a sequence produces one output. Example: text → sentiment.

• Many-to-many: a sequence in, a sequence out. Example: machine translation.

Example: sentiment analysis

Take the sentence “The movie was absolutely amazing.” The RNN reads it one word at a time, updating its memory after each word. Only at the end does it produce a verdict:

A many-to-one RNN reads the whole sentence before deciding.

Each word nudges the hidden state. “absolutely” intensifies whatever comes next, and “amazing” tips the balance. By the final step the hidden state holds a summary of the whole sentence, and that summary is what produces “Positive.”

Example: next-word prediction

Now a many-to-many setup. After every word, the RNN predicts what comes next.

Given “I am learning”, the most likely next word might be “deep”. Then given “I am learning deep”, the natural next word is “learning”. The previous words provide the context that makes the prediction sensible. This is also the basic idea behind language models.

The problem with long-term dependencies

Basic RNNs have one famous weakness. Consider:

“I grew up in India. … [many words later] … I speak fluent ___.”

The clue is far back in the sequence. A short-term dependency is when the relevant information is only a few steps away (easy for an RNN). A long-term dependency is when it’s many steps away, and that’s where basic RNNs struggle. The memory gets overwritten a little at every step, and the faint trace of an early word can be gone by the time we need it.

Vanishing gradients

The reason is mathematical, and it shows up during BPTT. To send the error back through ten time steps, the gradient is multiplied by a factor at every step. If that factor is smaller than 1, the signal shrinks again and again:

Gradient → × small → × small → × small → … → almost zero

With a factor of 0.5 per step, after 10 steps the gradient is only 0.⁵¹⁰ ≈ 0.001, about a thousandth of its original size. The earliest time steps get almost no learning signal, so the network can’t learn to connect them to the outcome.

Exploding gradients

The opposite can happen too. If the repeated factor is larger than 1, the gradient grows instead:

Gradient → × large → × large → × large → … → huge

With a factor of 2 per step, ten steps back gives ²¹⁰ = 1,024 times the original gradient. That leads to unstable training, enormous weight updates, and sometimes a loss that turns into NaN. A common fix is gradient clipping: if the gradient gets bigger than a chosen threshold, scale it down before applying the update. Vanishing gradients are harder to fix, which is what motivated the LSTM in the next article.

Advantages of RNNs

• Designed for sequential data.

• Maintain information from previous steps.

• Can handle variable-length sequences.

• Useful for time-dependent problems.

Limitations of RNNs

• Difficulty with long-term memory.

• Vanishing gradients.

• Exploding gradients.

• Sequential computation can be slow, since step 5 must wait for step 4.

  • Hard to parallelize across time steps.
A simple Python example

Let’s teach a tiny RNN to continue a pattern: given [10, 20, 30, 40], predict 50. We’ll train on many sequences that climb by a constant step, but deliberately leave out the exact [10, 20, 30, 40] one so we can test on it.

import numpy as np

import tensorflow as tf

from tensorflow.keras import layers, models, optimizers

# 1) Build training data: 4 numbers in, the next number out

X, y = [], []

for start in range(1, 21):

for step in range(1, 11):

if (start, step) == (10, 10): # held out for testing

continue

seq = [start + step * i for i in range(4)]

X.append(seq)

y.append(start + step * 4)

# Shape must be (samples, time steps, features); scale to small values

X = np.array(X, dtype=”float32")[…, None] / 100.0

y = np.array(y, dtype=”float32") / 100.0

# 2) Create the RNN

model = models.Sequential([

layers.Input(shape=(4, 1)),

layers.SimpleRNN(16), # the recurrent layer with 16 hidden units

layers.Dense(1), # turns the final hidden state into a number

])

model.compile(optimizer=optimizers.Adam(0.01), loss=”mse”)

# 3) Train

model.fit(X, y, epochs=300, batch_size=32, verbose=0)

# 4) Predict on the unseen sequence

test = np.array([[10, 20, 30, 40]], dtype=”float32")[…, None] / 100.0

print(model.predict(test)[0, 0] * 100) # should be close to 50

A few details worth understanding. The data shape (samples, time steps, features) is how Keras expects sequences. The SimpleRNN(16) layer has 16 × 1 input weights, 16 × 16 recurrent weights and 16 biases, which is 288 parameters in total. And scaling the numbers down matters, because large raw values push tanh into its flat regions where learning stalls. The prediction should land close to 50 but won’t be exactly 50. If it’s well off, train for more epochs.

Want to see clipping? Change the optimizer to optimizers.Adam(0.01, clipnorm=1.0).

Where are RNNs used?

• Speech recognition

• Sentiment analysis

• Text generation

• Time-series forecasting

• Language modeling

• Sequence classification

• Machine translation

A note on the present day: because of the limits above, many modern systems use LSTMs, GRUs and Transformers instead of basic RNNs, especially where long-range memory matters. Basic RNNs are still the best place to learn the core idea.

Common beginner questions

What is the hidden state? A vector of numbers that summarizes everything the network has seen so far in the sequence.

Is hidden state the same as memory? Roughly, yes, as an analogy. But it’s a compressed, constantly overwritten summary, not a filing cabinet of exact past inputs.

Why are RNN weights shared? So the same learned rule applies at every time step. It keeps the model small and lets it handle sequences of any length.

What is BPTT? Backpropagation applied to the unrolled network, sending the error back through each time step.

Why do RNNs have vanishing gradients? Because the gradient is multiplied by similar factors at every step going back, and repeated multiplication by numbers below 1 shrinks it toward zero.

Can RNNs remember everything? No. Basic RNNs mostly remember recent information well and distant information poorly.

RNN vs CNN? CNNs find local patterns in grids like images. RNNs process ordered sequences with a running memory.

RNN vs LSTM? An LSTM is an RNN with extra machinery (gates) that decides what to keep, forget and output, which helps it remember over long distances.

Conclusion

RNNs introduced the idea of giving neural networks a form of memory, allowing them to process information where sequence and order matter.

But basic RNNs struggle to hold on to information over long sequences. So how could we build a network that can decide what to remember, what to forget, and what to use?

This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

A new contest pits competitors against each other in a race to biological youth

—Jessica Hamzelou

This week, I officially signed up for an unusual competition. One that rewards competitors for getting younger.

I recently turned 40, and I don’t need reminding that both time and my chronological age only tick forward. But this game is focused on competitors’ biological ages, figures that are meant to provide a better way to measure the age-related health of our organs and bodies.

Over six months, around 500 of us will try to reverse our biological age using a bunch of different measures. There’s even a leaderboard! But is it even possible to measure whether someone is getting younger? 

Read the full story on the controversy around biological age measurements and how I’ll test them myself.

This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.

Opinion: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason

—Thore Graepel

Ten years ago, I watched a program I helped build stun the world by beating Go champion Lee Sedol. AlphaGo won after making a move so strange that some commentators thought it was a programming glitch. It was AlphaGo’s powers of reasoning that made this creative choice—and these are powers that today’s AI lacks. 

This is why I recently left my position at Google DeepMind. I believe we need a fresh approach to machine reasoning, one that draws on AlphaGo’s architecture.

Here’s why today’s AI doesn’t really reason—and what it would take to change that.

Thore Graepel is chair of machine learning at University College London. He was a core member of the AlphaGo team at DeepMind.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 OpenAI says rogue agents may have affected more than 100 organizations
The company is searching 50 petabytes of data for incidents. (Reuters $)
+ It says none of the incidents matched the Hugging Face attack. (Gizmodo)
+ OpenAI has fired three workers for allegedly mishandling information. (BBC)
+ California has subpoenaed OpenAI over its rogue AI agents. (Guardian)
+ Who’s liable when AI agents go rogue? (MIT Technology Review)

2 A US man allegedly smuggled $300 million of Nvidia chips to China
He’s been arrested in California on federal charges. (Reuters $)
+ The chip smuggling cases expose Nvidia’s blind spots. (Bloomberg $)
+ China plans to teach AI in every school by 2030. (WP $)
+ But it already has an overuse problem. (NYT $) 

3 Florida officials have found 11 Flock cameras with unknown owners
They don’t know who installed them or who has their data. (WP $)
+ Lawmakers are considering new regulations on Flock cameras. (Axios)
+ Here’s what Flock’s defenders are missing. (MIT Technology Review)

4 Ukraine has developed an acoustic fence that can cut drone cables
Acoustic sensors detect drones before hooks trap their cables. (New Scientist $)
+ Drone data from Ukraine is fueling a wild market. (MIT Technology Review)

5 A new AI “speech clock” can assess how fast you’re ageing
It uses hundreds of vocal features to estimate biological age. (Nature)
+ Aging clocks aim to predict how long you’ll live. (MIT Technology Review)

6 “Underwater umbrellas” could help corals survive hotter oceans
The shades protected corals during intense heat stress. (Gizmodo)

7 Apple’s upcoming smart home camera reportedly won’t record video
It will instead only give users text event descriptions. (Verge)

8 Retired humanoid robots are being trained to jump into molten steel
A Terminator-style death protects IP. (IE)

9 A man faces years in prison after AI slop caused a crocodile panic
Officials spent days searching for his AI-generated crocodile. (Futurism)

10 Finally, a laser mosquito killer is entering the market
Chinese startup Photon Matrix Lab plans to start shipments this month. (SCMP)

Quote of the day

“Those agents are doing exactly what they’ve been asked to do. They were supposed to be in sandboxes, but the sandboxes were leaky and horribly designed.”

—Yann LeCun, a Turing Award winner and former Meta chief AI scientist, tells Fortune that human error can be the real culprit behind the recent wave of AI agents going rogue.

One more thing


NASA is building the first nuclear reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft. How will it work?

Just before Artemis II began its historic slingshot around the moon, NASA revealed an even grander space travel plan. By the end of 2028, the agency aims to fly a nuclear reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft to Mars.

A successful mission would herald a new era in spaceflight—and might just give the US the edge in the race against China. But the project remains shrouded in mystery.

MIT Technology Review picked the brains of nuclear power and propulsion experts to find out how the nuclear-powered spacecraft might work. Here’s what we discovered.

—Robin George Andrews

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

+ Atlas Obscura has mapped out the oldest living things on Earth.
+ Brain scans show that dogs understand our emotions better than we thought.
+ Step into Springfield in miniature with this astonishing model featuring 76 locations from The Simpsons.
+ Minnesota’s State Fair has unleashed a crop of gloriously weird new foods, from Pickle pie to mustache pretzels.

items.title: Where every US governor stands on AI and the data-center boom
items.summary: Some state governors are bigger advocates for AI and data centers than others. Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images Midterm elections are right around the corner, with Election Day on November 3. Artificial intelligence and the data-center boom have pushed their way into the political arena. US governors' views range from exploring an AI "kill switch" to welcoming data centers. It's up to voters whether artificial intelligence will play a role in the outcome of the coming midterm elections . The AI boom — and the infrastructure needed to power it — has slowly become a flashpoint in US politics. The debate ranges from AI safety, regulation, and deepfakes to the rapid expansion of data centers . Many Big Tech firms advocate for faster expansion, while local residents have pushed back against data-center projects over their potential environmental and energy-cost impacts. One big question for voters: What roles should state and federal governments play in regulating AI? Another is how much power local communities should have over the data centers increasingly being built in their backyards. Governors across the political spectrum — 17 of whom are up for reelection this year — have taken varied approaches to the AI boom. All 39 gubernatorial races, across 36 states and three territories, are on November 3. Some governors, including California's Gavin Newsom (D) and New York's Kathy Hochul (D), are exploring an AI " kill switch " that would disable advanced AI systems in an out-of-control event. Republican Utah Gov. Spencer Cox has also called for federal AI safety rules. Others, including the Republican governors of Nevada and North Dakota and the Democratic governors of Michigan and New Mexico — whose states have major AI-computing projects under construction — see data centers as an economic opportunity. Here's what every US governor has said so far about AI, data centers, or both. Alabama Stew Milne/Getty Images Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey (R) has approached AI as an opportunity to improve government, but one that needs guardrails. In 2024, she created a statewide generative AI task force to examine how it could be used within the state government, emphasizing both the usage of AI and transparency, privacy, and public safety. "GenAI represents a monumental step forward in the potential for our state government to serve the public," Ivey said in a 2024 statement . "However, its capabilities must first be studied carefully to ensure it is implemented in the most responsible and efficient manner possible." She is one of the few governors across the US who have taken a harder line on Chinese AI tools. In 2025, Ivey issued a ban on Chinese-affiliated artificial intelligence platforms DeepSeek and Manus from all state-owned devices and networks. Alaska Michael Dunleavy is the governor of Alaska. Bloomberg/Getty Images Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) has pitched the state as a potential hub for the AI boom and the computing infrastructure needed for it, arguing that Alaska has an "arctic advantage." Dunleavy has said he believes Alaska's colder climate can significantly reduce the cost of cooling AI server racks, saying in late 2025 that an Alaskan 1-gigawatt campus could save operators up to $150 million annually in cooling costs compared to a warmer state. Dunleavy has also said that data centers could be an economic driver for Alaska, particularly by creating more construction jobs across the state. He frequently uses AI, too , incorporating certain tools into his work as governor, including using the technology during meetings. Arizona Katie Hobbs is the governor of Arizona. Mario Tama/Getty Images Katie Hobbs (D), Arizona's governor up for reelection, has largely framed AI as an economic opportunity that the state needs to prepare for, rather than turn away from. Hobbs has said she does not support a moratorium , which is a temporary pause, on new data-center development. At the same time, she has pushed for more structure around AI. Her administration created the state's first AI steering committee in 2025 and launched an AI government tool in 2026, and she has described the goal as ensuring AI strengthens rather than undermines the state's economy. "Arizona has built one of the strongest AI ecosystems in the country, and our community colleges help power it," Hobbs wrote in a January 22 post on X. Arkansas Sarah Huckabee Sanders is the governor of Arkansas. USDA Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R), who is up for reelection, has said she believes AI has the potential to strengthen government efficiency, but it requires proper policies and regulations. "AI is changing how we work, interact, and find information — and Arkansas can't afford to be left behind," she wrote in a statement in February following a new state AI effectiveness and safety report . The report, which was completed by an AI working group that Sanders launched in 2024, found that AI could help the state improve Medicaid and SNAP programs and expand other digital services. Earlier this year, she also joined RAISE US, a national artificial intelligence initiative launched by former Indiana governor Eric Holcomb and former US Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo. The initiative intends to partner with governors, employers, workers and training organizations to help the workforce transition to an AI economy. She was one of several politicians who urged Congress to remove the AI regulatory moratorium from the One, Big, Beautiful Bill in 2025. California Gavin Newsom is the governor of California. Sean Rayford/Getty Images California's Gavin Newsom (D) has moved from a more cautious approach to AI regulation toward some of the most aggressive AI-safety proposals in the country. After vetoing an AI safety bill in 2024, Newsom has since signed legislation creating independent oversight and auditing requirements on AI systems. Now, Newsom is backing the idea of an AI " kill switch, " which would be an emergency shutoff for frontier AI models, as part of a September executive order. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has proposed a similar idea. Newsom has also directed experts to consider independent verification of AI companies' safety systems, arguing that California should move ahead even as federal action remains limited. Colorado Jared Polis is the governor of Colorado. Hyoung Chang/The Denver Post Colorado Gov. Jared Polis (D) signed Senate Bill 24-205 in 2024, making Colorado the first state to enact a comprehensive consumer-protection law aimed at protecting consumers from AI-driven algorithmic discrimination in areas such as employment, housing, education, and healthcare. That bill was later repealed by Polis this year, however. In his repeal, he narrowed the state's framework by mandating specific transparency, documentation, and consumer rights when automated tools "materially influence" consequential decisions. The new bill will take effect on January 1, 2027. Polis has also shown some support for a federal moratorium on state AI laws restricting artificial intelligence , according to a 2025 Bloomberg article. Connecticut Ned Lamont is the governor of Connecticut. Tyler Russell/Connecticut Public via Getty Images Ned Lamont (D), governor of Connecticut and up for reelection, signed a bipartisan AI bill earlier this year addressing youth online safety . Lamont's approach is focused on preparing people to work alongside AI rather than restricting its use. He's also invested in workforce training designed to help Connecticut workers compete for jobs in the tech market: In February, he launched the third phase of the state's Tech Talent Accelerator, a program that aims to expand AI education and workforce training. Delaware Meg Oliphant/Getty Images Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer (D) has sought to make the state a place where companies can experiment with AI without abandoning regulation. In 2025, he signed legislation launching an AI regulatory sandbox where companies can test AI technologies under government oversight, particularly in corporate governance, health care, biotechnology and financial services. Meyer has described the sandbox as a way to combine innovation with transparency and public trust. "This initiative creates space for visionaries and risk-takers to responsibly test cutting-edge artificial intelligence technologies in Delaware—prioritizing transparency, public trust, and thoughtful oversight," he wrote in a statement. Florida Ron DeSantis is the governor of Florida. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images Ron DeSantis (R), Florida's governor, has pushed for protections around AI rather than banning the technology or leaving it unregulated. His proposed AI Bill of Rights in late 2025 included data-privacy protections, parental controls, consumer disclosures and restrictions on using someone's name, image or likeness without consent. "The AI Bill of Rights defends consumers, medical patients, and families in Florida from the potential harms of artificial intelligence applications," he wrote on X in March . "It is especially important that we protect the most vulnerable among us: our children." Regarding data centers, DeSantis signed a bill earlier this year that would prevent residents from bearing the costs of hyperscale data centers through utility bills and give local governments more authority over where those facilities are built. Georgia Brian Kemp is the governor of Georgia. Derek White/Getty Images for The Coca Cola Company Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp (R) sees AI as an economic opportunity the state cannot afford to ignore. He has backed the expansion of data centers and has positioned Georgia as a potential hub for the country's AI infrastructure, meeting directly with OpenAI and Georgia Power in July to discuss OpenAI's activity in the state, sites of interest, jobs, and investment commitments. Much of his approach has focused on building the electricity and infrastructure needed to attract AI investment to the state. Hawaii Josh Green is the governor of Hawaii. Jason Andrew for The Washington Post via Getty Images Hawaii Gov. Josh Green (D), up for reelection, has taken a cautious approach to AI. In July, he signed legislation establishing new safety measures for it — particularly surrounding 'deepfakes', which imitate one's voice and face — saying AI presents "fascinating opportunities" but that the state needs to be intentional about recognizing its potential dangers. Idaho Brad Little is the governor of Idaho. Bloomberg/Getty Images Idaho Gov. Brad Little (R), who is up for reelection, has focused heavily on preparing students for an AI-driven economy. In March, his administration launched a partnership with Microsoft, Micron and other technology companies to teach K-12 students and teachers how to adopt AI into the classroom. While Micron will teach teachers how to use AI, Microsoft will provide AI literacy programs and its chatbot, Copilot, for all students over 13 and teachers. Illinois JB Pritzker is the governor of Illinois. John Nacion/Getty Images JB Pritzker, Illinois' governor up for reelection, views artificial intelligence as a transformative tool that also poses severe, existential risks to humanity. "It's time to sound the alarm — louder — on reining in Artificial Intelligence," Pritzker wrote in an early September statement. "It's becoming more clear the threat AI poses to humanity, so I'm calling for immediate action from the industry and Washington. When AI researchers are whistleblowing, we need to listen." His statement urged a stop to Big Tech's lobbying against safety, Congressional hearings on AI safety, and more. Pritzker also established an AI cabinet in September to assess the various safety risks posed by AI. Indiana Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Mike Braun (R), Indiana's governor, views AI as an economic opportunity to boost wages, create jobs, and to position Indiana as a leader in AI's adoption. In April, he launched an initiative titled IN AI to help Indiana businesses understand where AI can improve their work, how to access and use different AI tools, and where to find employees across the state who understand the technology. He has publicly cautioned against building data centers in the state that drain Indiana's water resources. The state is home to two large data-center projects in the US, however, housing Meta's data center that is expected to deliver 1 gigawatt of capacity and span 1,500 acres in Lebanon, as well as Google's Fort Wayne Data Center, which will require up to 1.2 gigawatts of power at full build-out. Iowa Kim Reynolds is the governor of Iowa. Charlie Neibergall/Getty Images In February , Iowa's Gov. Kim Reynolds banned DeepSeek and RedNote, two Chinese-owned apps, from state devices. She also prohibited all state agencies from subscribing to or having an account on either app. Reynolds has shown a focus on how to responsibly adopt AI, signing an Act in May that regulates AI chatbots , particularly for minors. One of the regulations in the Act provides disclaimers at the beginning of each chat and once every three hours. Kansas Laura Kelly is the governor of Kansas. Michael B. Thomas/Getty Images Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly (D) supports a regulated approach to AI that balances the innovation it brings. In August, Kelly told the Topeka Capital-Journal that there needs to be guardrails around data center construction and the water and energy use associated with them. In August 2023 , she created an AI policy that requires reviews of accuracy, appropriateness, privacy, and security before any action is taken or information is shared. Kentucky Andy Beshear is the governor of Kentucky. John Nacion/Getty Images Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) is an advocate for federal oversight and regulation of AI to balance its benefits with risks such as national security and job displacement. He signed an executive order in August to mitigate the potential environmental and cost impacts of data centers. Specifically, the order requires the companies building the data centers to submit a plan to the state's Energy and Environment Cabinet detailing how they will cover their full energy costs. Louisiana Jeff Landry is the governor of Louisiana. Win McNamee/Getty Images Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry (R) also views AI as a way to drive economic growth, but said it poses security and utility cost risks. In June, Landry issued an executive order requiring data centers seeking state sales-tax breaks to protect ratepayers from higher electricity costs, unless the state determines the project's other benefits outweigh the higher electricity costs. In 2025, Landry, like Iowa's governor, also signed an executive order banning China's DeepSeek across all state agencies. "As technology advances, so do the threats," he wrote in a statement . "This executive order ensures we are protecting our people, our data, and our national security from the CCP's growing influence in AI." The state is home to one of the largest planned data centers in the US, housing Meta's Hyperion AI data center, a more than $50 billion investment that will span more than 3,600 acres and is planned to deliver 5 gigawatts of capacity once fully developed. Maine Janet Mills is the governor of Maine. Bloomberg/Getty Images Maine Gov. Janet Mills (D) has taken a more cautious approach toward the growing AI industry. This year, Mills vetoed a bipartisan bill that would have placed a temporary pause on data center construction requiring 20 or more megawatts of power. She's also said she supported a federal moratorium if it had exempted a specific project that she believed could bring jobs to Maine. In June 2025, Mills signed a bill that bans companies from using chatbots without clear disclosure. The bill also added AI-generated deepfakes to the state's revenge porn laws. Maryland Wes Moore is the governor of Maryland. Jamie Sabau/Getty Images Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D), who is up for reelection, signed an executive order in early September that relieves locals of the costs of the centers' energy usage, includes environmental protection efforts and AI job training, and establishes a "public dashboard" where locals can express their input on the centers. Moore's executive order also established the Maryland Data Center Task Force, which will review data center projects, maintain a public data center dashboard, and more. "My fear is a technology that no human being can control," Moore told MS NOW reporters in late September . "We've got to understand that delicate balance of cooperation and competition. As a governor, I'm very competitive with my other governors. But I do understand that there are places where the focus is cooperation and not competition." Massachusetts Maura Healey is the governor of Massachusetts. David L. Ryan/The Boston Globe via Getty Images Maura Healey (D), Massachusetts' governor up for reelection, has argued that AI shouldn't advance faster than the government can protect people from its risks. In September, Healey called for federal action to strengthen AI guardrails and oversight that both allow for innovation and protect national security. Like Moore, Healey's administration has also created a state AI task force. The state's task force, created in 2024, also includes a $100 million Applied AI Hub that studies how to apply AI to advance Massachusetts' life sciences, healthcare, financial services, advanced manufacturing, robotics, and education sectors. "AI has enormous potential to drive scientific discovery, strengthen key industries, improve public services, and create new opportunities for businesses and residents across Massachusetts," Gov. Healey wrote in a September press release . "At the same time, the rapid pace of AI development raises serious concerns about safety, accountability, privacy, civil rights, the future of work, and public trust." Michigan Gretchen Whitmer is the governor of Michigan. Bloomberg/Getty Images Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D) has welcomed data center construction, such as Oracle and OpenAI's project in Saline Township, but with guidelines. Her July action plan ensures that data center companies pay construction and operation costs, strengthen and safeguard the state's electric grid and natural resources, and are accountable for their development. "It's simple: any data center company that wants to invest in Michigan must ensure working families do not pay a single penny for data center development or operations, protect our natural resources, and create local, good-paying jobs," Whitmer wrote in a press release. Michigan is home to The Barn , a $16 billion, 1.4-gigawatt data-center campus in Saline Township that Related Digital is building for Oracle and OpenAI as part of the Stargate project. Minnesota Tim Walz is the governor of Minnesota. Salih Okuroglu/Anadolu via Getty Images Tim Walz (D), Minnesota's governor, signed a law in May prohibiting access to "nudification" technology that can generate fake nude images of real people. "This bill makes clear that using technology to create fake, non-consensual intimate images is unacceptable and puts Minnesota at the forefront of addressing the harms of AI while protecting people from exploitation and abuse," Walz wrote in a press release. The law echoes Walz's broader approach to AI, which encourages its development while drawing lines around any usage that threatens privacy or safety, specifically for children. In May 2023, he also signed a state law that regulates and restricts the use of deepfakes in political campaigns . Mississippi Tate Reeves is the governor of Mississippi. Bloomberg/Getty Images Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves (R) signed a memorandum of understanding with NVIDIA in June 2025 to promote AI education, workforce integration, and research collaboration. His focus is on ensuring Mississippi's workforce can use AI effectively; in May, he launched a statewide AI framework that centers on equipping students and workers with skills in ethical reasoning and AI-related cybersecurity awareness. During a Sept. 30 Federalist Society conversation, Reeves emphasized that Mississippi works efficiently at cutting deals with companies, particularly AI and data center companies, highlighting the state's $20 billion partnership with xAI was expected to launch only a few weeks after making the deal. "So many states around the country start at no and give you the burden to ultimately get to yes…" Reeves said. "…We start at yes, and as we navigate our way through it, we've got very seasoned, talented people who run our economic development shop." Missouri Mike Kehoe is the governor of Missouri. Mark Schiefelbein-Pool/Getty Images In May, Mike Kehoe (R), Missouri's governor, announced that Google will invest $15 billion into data center construction in New Florence, a rural town in central Missouri. Kehoe also signed an executive order in January that allows for growth in data centers and Missouri's use in AI, while calling on economic and natural resources directors to study how AI could impact the local workforce and citizens' energy bills. The state is home to one of the largest planned data centers in the US, Nebius' AI Factory, which will reach a capacity of up to 1.2 gigawatts. Montana Greg Gianforte is the governor of Montana. Michael Ciaglo/Getty Images Greg Gianforte (R), Montana's governor and a former software entrepreneur who founded RightNow Technologies, later acquired by Oracle, has approached AI from a business perspective. In 2025, he signed Montana's Right to Compute Act, which established legal protections for businesses' use of AI, limiting the government's interference in their use. He also launched 406 JOBS in 2025, a workforce program aimed at modernizing the state's workforce. Nebraska Jim Pillen is the governor of Nebraska. USDA Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen (R), up for reelection, like several other governors, has expressed that locals shouldn't front the bill for energy costs stemming from data centers. In July, Pillen ended access to certain state tax incentives for data centers and created a task force to examine their impact on water, electricity, and local infrastructure. "Early in my administration, I called for a pause in building new data centers, and this executive order is consistent with that call," Pillen wrote in a press release. "Data centers are a booming industry. Major tech companies are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into them. And while that presents significant economic opportunity, it also presents resource challenges." Nevada Joe Lombardo is the governor of Nevada. Bloomberg/Getty Images Joe Lombardo (R), Nevada's governor up for reelection, has emphasized the economic opportunity AI data centers bring for the state. In September, he signed an executive order requiring data center developers to cover project-related energy costs. The order also aims to support public schools and protect the state's water resources. Lombardo has said he supports data centers because they bring jobs, investment, and economic growth to the state. "At the same time, we have to put the right parameters in place to ensure they don't raise costs on Nevada residents or businesses," he wrote in a May Facebook post . "As Governor, I'm focused on growing our economy responsibly while protecting rates for families." New Hampshire Kelly Ayotte is the governor of New Hampshire. Suzanne Kreiter/The Boston Globe via Getty Images New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte (R), who is up for reelection, has shown skepticism toward data centers due to the amount of energy they require. In August, Ayotte said she supported a moratorium on data centers , arguing that New Hampshire does not have enough energy capacity to support them without hiking up electricity costs. She also said she is opposed to a potential data center being built in Bow, a small town in central New Hampshire. New Jersey Mikie Sherrill is the governor of New Jersey. Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images In September, New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) issued a $1.07 million fine to the DataOne data center in Vineland, holding that the data center violated the New Jersey Air Pollution Control Act by installing and operating 62 large natural-gas power generators without Department of Environmental Protection permits. "Data centers will pay their fair share for energy, be accountable for their water and energy use, protect our environment, create good-paying union jobs, and invest in communities," Sherrill wrote on a social media post. She has signed legislation requiring data centers to report their electricity and water consumption to the Board of Public Utilities every six months , and also has expressed that AI instruction should be embedded into New Jersey's education programs . New Mexico Michelle Lujan Grisham is the governor of New Mexico. MAURO PIMENTEL/AFP via Getty Images In 2025, Michelle Lujan Grisham (D), New Mexico's governor, announced a $1 billion partnership with Meta on a new geothermal plant for the company's data center. Geothermal energy, which is considered a green power source, taps heat beneath Earth's surface to generate electricity; it can also be used directly for heating and cooling. The $1 billion investment will create 3,000 construction jobs and 100 jobs running the geothermal power plant. New Mexico touts 22 data centers — one of which is Project Jupiter , one of the largest in the US. The state is home to one of the largest planned data centers in the US, Stargate's Project Jupiter, which could include up to 2.45 gigawatts of Bloom Energy fuel cells, replacing an earlier proposal centered on gas turbines and diesel generators. New York Kathy Hochul is the governor of New York. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images Kathy Hochul (D), New York's governor up for reelection, like California Gov. Gavin Newsom, is exploring an AI " kill switch " that would shut off AI systems in a critical event. In late December 2025, she signed the RAISE Act , which requires AI developers to create and publish information about their safety protocols and to report incidents to the state government within 72 hours of an incident. Under the law, New York's Attorney General can bring civil actions against developers who fail to submit reports, with penalties rising up to $1 million for the first violation and up to $3 million for subsequent violations. Hochul also issued an executive order imposing a one-year moratorium on large-scale AI data centers in July to evaluate and address their environmental and community impact. North Carolina Josh Stein is the governor of North Carolina. Bloomberg/Getty Images North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein (D), like many governors, has approached AI as both an economic opportunity and a policy challenge. His administration's AI Strategic Roadmap , launched in July, aims to protect locals from any harm AI might cause, prepare workers for AI-related changes, and use AI to improve government work. In a speech announcing the roadmap , Stein said AI can help with government efficiency, such as scanning outdated documents and answering residents' questions, but also emphasized the need to address the risks that come with its usage. North Dakota Kelly Armstrong is the governor of North Dakota. Bryan Bedder/Getty Images for Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library Kelly Armstrong (R), North Dakota's governor, signed legislation in 2025 that limits the role of AI in certain health-care decisions , requiring licensed physicians, rather than algorithms, to make final decisions in some cases. Armstrong also sees AI as an economic opportunity, holding that North Dakota's natural-gas industry could help supply the energy data centers need. Similar to Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, Armstrong believes the state's colder climate can allow AI and data center companies to lower their cooling costs. Ohio Mike DeWine is the governor of Ohio. Bloomberg/Getty Images Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) said in September that the federal government should enact regulations on AI, not the states. "Look, as far as AI, this really needs to come from the federal government," DeWine said at an event in New Albany, near Columbus. "We need to have uniformity, not just in this country; we need to have uniformity in the world. So, I would certainly hope we can see some uniformity coming out of Washington." In May, he also paused new applications for data center tax exemptions amid growing scrutiny of the state's incentives and the costs associated with large facilities. According to the governor, in 2025, data centers that had been granted sales and use tax benefits in the state reported a total capital investment of $27.2 billion. The state is home to one of the largest planned data centers in the US, housing Nvidia-backed project PORTS-Pike Technology Campus, which is expected to include up to 10 gigawatts of data-center capacity. Oklahoma Kevin Stitt is the governor of Oklahoma. Heather Diehl/Getty Images Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt (R) created an AI task force in 2023 to study how the technology could improve government efficiency, education, and workforce development, and has repeatedly described Oklahoma as a potential AI hub. Stitt's task force was completed in 2024 and recommended five ways the state can implement AI into its workforce and government, largely by creating oversight, economic, digital, and talent workforce committees that encourage the use of AI across sectors. "Oklahoma is poised to lead the nation in implementation of artificial intelligence technology, and we have to capitalize on the momentum. Oklahoma truly could be the AI capital of the nation," Stitt wrote in a 2024 press release. Like other governors, he aims to protect ratepayers from increasing energy costs related to data centers, but also has stated that he supports the construction of data centers, highlighting property rights and the free market . Oregon Tina Kotek is the governor of Oregon. Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images Oregon's Tina Kotek (D), who is up for reelection, has said states cannot wait for federal action on AI. In September, Kotek issued an executive order similar to those of California Gov. Gavin Newsom and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, directing the state to assess the viability of a "kill switch" requirement for frontier AI models. "It's encouraging to hear AI companies are beginning to come forward with proposals to address safety concerns, but we cannot simply wait for the private sector to self-regulate a technology that poses such an existential and evolving risk," Kotek wrote in a press release. Pennsylvania Josh Shapiro is the governor of Pennsylvania. Gilbert Carrasquillo/GC Images Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D), up for reelection, said at a September AI Horizons Summit that he sees AI's potential to improve productivity and public services, but argued that the technology needs stronger guardrails. "I want to be clear: I am not a doomer," he said at the summit. "I don't think it is inevitable that AI is going to take over the world or that someone will misuse it to kill us or do harm." He also cracked down on data centers in August, saying that data center proposals are scaring and changing the character of Pennsylvania communities. Rhode Island Dan McKee is the governor of Rhode Island. Bloomberg/Getty Images Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee (D) created an AI task force and Center of Excellence for AI and Data in 2024, both in an effort to study how AI could increase government efficiency and improve public services. "Rhode Island recognizes that the rise of AI technology will enhance future government operations and change the way we do business," McKee wrote in a press release. "Rather than simply react to the changes in the information technology landscape, I want Rhode Island to be a leader as this field evolves." South Carolina Henry McMaster is the governor of South Carolina. Sean Rayford/Getty Images Beginning in early 2024, Henry McMaster (R), South Carolina's governor, was the chair of the Southern Regional Education Board Commission on Artificial Intelligence in Education. In his role, McMaster convened with other education and business leaders to chart a course for the use of AI in classrooms and to prepare the workforce for the technology. "When used correctly, AI is a powerful tool capable of reshaping our education system," McMaster wrote . "By working together, we can overcome the challenges that AI presents and harness its power to ensure our students are prepared for the workforce of the future." In general, McMaster is cautious toward rushing into government regulation on AI, arguing that politicians do not have a complete understanding yet of its benefits and drawbacks. Regarding his view on data centers, McMaster said in late September that he does not plan to call for a statewide data center moratorium. The state houses three of Google's data centers, which opened in 2007. In 2024, the company announced it would establish two new data center campuses in the state, a combined investment of $3.3 billion. "Google's latest investment will strengthen South Carolina's position as an emerging leader in technology and innovation," McMaster wrote in a statement . South Dakota Larry Rhoden is the governor of South Dakota. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden (R), who is up for reelection, has also banned Chinese apps from state devices. In 2025, Rhoden signed a bill making it a Class 1 misdemeanor to disseminate an undisclosed deepfake intended to injure a candidate within 90 days of an election, punishable by up to a year in jail, a $2,000 fine, or both. He is one of several governors who signed a bill that protects residents from increased utility costs caused by data centers. Tennessee Bill Lee is the governor of Tennessee. Brett Carlsen/Getty Images Bill Lee (R), Tennessee's governor, signed the ELVIS Act — Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security Act — in 2024 to protect musicians from being cloned or replicated by AI without consent. Tennessee was the first state in the US to legally protect artists and musicians from deepfakes. Lee also signed a bill earlier this year that prohibits AI developers from falsely posing as qualified mental health professionals. The state is home to one of the largest planned data centers in the US, xAI's Colossus 2, which powers Grok, the AI chatbot on X, and is expected to deliver 1.5 gigawatts in capacity. Texas Greg Abbott is the governor of Texas. Kelsey Brown/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), up for reelection, has shifted his views toward AI over the past year. Less than a year ago, Abbott welcomed the plethora of Big Tech companies constructing data centers across the state, calling Texas the " epicenter of AI development ." But with growing backlash toward the uptick in electric and water costs for locals, Abbott has shifted his perspective on data centers, saying that the companies building them " dug their own grave " by failing to also build community support. In August, Abbott announced that OpenAI would comply with his established data center guidelines, including not passing on costs to Texans or interfering with their quality of life. The state houses several of the US' largest planned data centers, including Meta's El Paso data center and Fermi America's Project Matador, the latter pursuing up to 17 gigawatts of private power. Utah Spencer Cox is the governor of Utah. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Utah Gov. Spencer Cox (R) called on Congress in September to establish guidelines on AI, including mandatory reporting of major safety incidents, whistleblower protections for tech employees, independent safety evaluations for models, and restrictions on the sale of advanced AI chips to China. "We can build the world's most advanced AI here in America while ensuring it remains firmly in service of humanity," Cox wrote on X . In May, he issued an order establishing a " higher bar " for future data center projects following public backlash against his support for a project near Salt Lake City . The order requires greater transparency and protections for water, air quality, the Great Salt Lake, local communities, and utility customers. Vermont Phil Scott is the governor of Vermont. JOSEPH PREZIOSO/AFP via Getty Images Vermont Gov. Phil Scott (R), who is up for reelection, is one of many governors who established a task force to assess how AI might shape the state's economy. In June, Scott's administration partnered with Anthropic through Vermont's Agency of Digital Services to test state IT systems for security vulnerabilities. The agreement gives the state $100,000 in credits for Claude Code, Anthropic's AI tool. He also signed legislation requiring disclosure of deceptive and fraudelent AI-generated content used in election campaigns within 90 days of an election. Virginia Abigail Spanberger is the governor of Virginia. Win McNamee/Getty Images Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger is one of several governors who believe states should lead on AI risk assessments rather than wait for Washington to act. "The federal government needs to play a much larger role in regulating this emerging technology to ensure its safe development and the protection of people and their livelihoods," Spanberger wrote in September . She created a state AI Task Force in September to examine workforce displacement, data privacy, cybersecurity, and ways existing laws can address AI-related harms. Regarding data centers, Virginia has the largest data market in the US with over 100,000 jobs and over $40 billion in investments, according to the Northern Virginia Technology Council. Spanberger recently unveiled a Data Center Accountability Framework , requiring centers to pay their own transmission costs, strengthen environmental and water-use protections, and give communities more input on proposed developments. Washington Alexi Rosenfeld/Getty Images Bob Ferguson (D), Washington's governor, has expressed concern over children's safety when using AI. Earlier this year, he signed legislation that requires disclosures that people are interacting with AI, safeguards around self-harm content, and protections for minors from sexually explicit conversations. Ferguson also signed a bill that requires covered AI providers to include provenance data in AI-generated or materially altered images, video, and audio. West Virginia Patrick Morrisey is the governor of West Virginia. Allison Joyce/Getty Images West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey (R) has said he views the state as a "powerhouse" for AI and cloud computing, announcing earlier this year that Penzance Management will invest $4 billion in an AI campus in Berkeley County, about 75 miles northwest of Washington, DC. "By earning the state's first High Impact Intelligence Center designation, Penzance is helping us transform the Mountain State into a powerhouse for artificial intelligence and cloud computing," he wrote in a statement. "This project brings a massive new revenue stream to our communities - all driven by private capital and our commitment to a business-friendly, reliable energy strategy." Morrisey has also supported AI health tools that reduce administrative work for rural providers. Wisconsin Tony Evers is the governor of Wisconsin. Daniel Boczarski/Getty Images for WisDems Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers (D) has focused his approach toward AI on how it affects the workforce. In 2023, he created the Governor's Task Force on Workforce and Artificial Intelligence to assess how the technology could reshape Wisconsin jobs, skills, and key industries. Its 2024 action plan focused on preparing workers and institutions for an AI-driven economy. He has also welcomed data center projects, saying they can be built while still protecting the environment and the local communities. Wyoming Mark Gordon, governor of Wyoming, during the DC Blockchain Summit in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, March 26, 2025. The summit brings together policymakers and top influencers to discuss the most important issues facing the crypto industry. Photographer: Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg via Getty Images Bloomberg/Getty Images Mark Gordon (R), Wyoming's governor, sees AI as an opportunity to grow the state's economy, especially through data centers and advanced computing. Earlier this year, he issued " Data Centers the Wyoming Way ," an executive order intended to create a statewide framework for data-center development, including its energy, water, and community impacts. "While other states hit the pause button out of political fear, we are choosing action and collaboration," Gov. Gordon wrote in a statement to Business Insider. "We are proving America's digital infrastructure can be built the Wyoming Way." Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Some state governors are bigger advocates for AI and data centers than others.

Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images

  • Midterm elections are right around the corner, with Election Day on November 3.
  • Artificial intelligence and the data-center boom have pushed their way into the political arena.
  • US governors' views range from exploring an AI "kill switch" to welcoming data centers.

It's up to voters whether artificial intelligence will play a role in the outcome of the coming midterm elections.

The AI boom — and the infrastructure needed to power it — has slowly become a flashpoint in US politics. The debate ranges from AI safety, regulation, and deepfakes to the rapid expansion of data centers.

Many Big Tech firms advocate for faster expansion, while local residents have pushed back against data-center projects over their potential environmental and energy-cost impacts.

One big question for voters: What roles should state and federal governments play in regulating AI? Another is how much power local communities should have over the data centers increasingly being built in their backyards.

Governors across the political spectrum — 17 of whom are up for reelection this year — have taken varied approaches to the AI boom. All 39 gubernatorial races, across 36 states and three territories, are on November 3.

Some governors, including California's Gavin Newsom (D) and New York's Kathy Hochul (D), are exploring an AI "kill switch" that would disable advanced AI systems in an out-of-control event. Republican Utah Gov. Spencer Cox has also called for federal AI safety rules.

Others, including the Republican governors of Nevada and North Dakota and the Democratic governors of Michigan and New Mexico — whose states have major AI-computing projects under construction — see data centers as an economic opportunity.

Here's what every US governor has said so far about AI, data centers, or both.

Alabama

Stew Milne/Getty Images

Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey (R) has approached AI as an opportunity to improve government, but one that needs guardrails.

In 2024, she created a statewide generative AI task force to examine how it could be used within the state government, emphasizing both the usage of AI and transparency, privacy, and public safety.

"GenAI represents a monumental step forward in the potential for our state government to serve the public," Ivey said in a 2024 statement. "However, its capabilities must first be studied carefully to ensure it is implemented in the most responsible and efficient manner possible."

She is one of the few governors across the US who have taken a harder line on Chinese AI tools. In 2025, Ivey issued a ban on Chinese-affiliated artificial intelligence platforms DeepSeek and Manus from all state-owned devices and networks.

Alaska
Michael Dunleavy is the governor of Alaska.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) has pitched the state as a potential hub for the AI boom and the computing infrastructure needed for it, arguing that Alaska has an "arctic advantage."

Dunleavy has said he believes Alaska's colder climate can significantly reduce the cost of cooling AI server racks, saying in late 2025 that an Alaskan 1-gigawatt campus could save operators up to $150 million annually in cooling costs compared to a warmer state.

Dunleavy has also said that data centers could be an economic driver for Alaska, particularly by creating more construction jobs across the state.

He frequently uses AI, too, incorporating certain tools into his work as governor, including using the technology during meetings.

Arizona
Katie Hobbs is the governor of Arizona.

Mario Tama/Getty Images

Katie Hobbs (D), Arizona's governor up for reelection, has largely framed AI as an economic opportunity that the state needs to prepare for, rather than turn away from.

Hobbs has said she does not support a moratorium, which is a temporary pause, on new data-center development. At the same time, she has pushed for more structure around AI.

Her administration created the state's first AI steering committee in 2025 and launched an AI government tool in 2026, and she has described the goal as ensuring AI strengthens rather than undermines the state's economy.

"Arizona has built one of the strongest AI ecosystems in the country, and our community colleges help power it," Hobbs wrote in a January 22 post on X.

Arkansas
Sarah Huckabee Sanders is the governor of Arkansas.

USDA

Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R), who is up for reelection, has said she believes AI has the potential to strengthen government efficiency, but it requires proper policies and regulations.

"AI is changing how we work, interact, and find information — and Arkansas can't afford to be left behind," she wrote in a statement in February following a new state AI effectiveness and safety report.

The report, which was completed by an AI working group that Sanders launched in 2024, found that AI could help the state improve Medicaid and SNAP programs and expand other digital services.

Earlier this year, she also joined RAISE US, a national artificial intelligence initiative launched by former Indiana governor Eric Holcomb and former US Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo. The initiative intends to partner with governors, employers, workers and training organizations to help the workforce transition to an AI economy.

She was one of several politicians who urged Congress to remove the AI regulatory moratorium from the One, Big, Beautiful Bill in 2025.

California
Gavin Newsom is the governor of California.

Sean Rayford/Getty Images

California's Gavin Newsom (D) has moved from a more cautious approach to AI regulation toward some of the most aggressive AI-safety proposals in the country.

After vetoing an AI safety bill in 2024, Newsom has since signed legislation creating independent oversight and auditing requirements on AI systems.

Now, Newsom is backing the idea of an AI "kill switch," which would be an emergency shutoff for frontier AI models, as part of a September executive order. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has proposed a similar idea.

Newsom has also directed experts to consider independent verification of AI companies' safety systems, arguing that California should move ahead even as federal action remains limited.

Colorado
Jared Polis is the governor of Colorado.

Hyoung Chang/The Denver Post

Colorado Gov. Jared Polis (D) signed Senate Bill 24-205 in 2024, making Colorado the first state to enact a comprehensive consumer-protection law aimed at protecting consumers from AI-driven algorithmic discrimination in areas such as employment, housing, education, and healthcare.

That bill was later repealed by Polis this year, however. In his repeal, he narrowed the state's framework by mandating specific transparency, documentation, and consumer rights when automated tools "materially influence" consequential decisions.

The new bill will take effect on January 1, 2027.

Polis has also shown some support for a federal moratorium on state AI laws restricting artificial intelligence, according to a 2025 Bloomberg article.

Connecticut
Ned Lamont is the governor of Connecticut.

Tyler Russell/Connecticut Public via Getty Images

Ned Lamont (D), governor of Connecticut and up for reelection, signed a bipartisan AI bill earlier this year addressing youth online safety.

Lamont's approach is focused on preparing people to work alongside AI rather than restricting its use. He's also invested in workforce training designed to help Connecticut workers compete for jobs in the tech market: In February, he launched the third phase of the state's Tech Talent Accelerator, a program that aims to expand AI education and workforce training.

Delaware

Meg Oliphant/Getty Images

Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer (D) has sought to make the state a place where companies can experiment with AI without abandoning regulation.

In 2025, he signed legislation launching an AI regulatory sandbox where companies can test AI technologies under government oversight, particularly in corporate governance, health care, biotechnology and financial services.

Meyer has described the sandbox as a way to combine innovation with transparency and public trust.

"This initiative creates space for visionaries and risk-takers to responsibly test cutting-edge artificial intelligence technologies in Delaware—prioritizing transparency, public trust, and thoughtful oversight," he wrote in a statement.

Florida
Ron DeSantis is the governor of Florida.

Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

Ron DeSantis (R), Florida's governor, has pushed for protections around AI rather than banning the technology or leaving it unregulated.

His proposed AI Bill of Rights in late 2025 included data-privacy protections, parental controls, consumer disclosures and restrictions on using someone's name, image or likeness without consent.

"The AI Bill of Rights defends consumers, medical patients, and families in Florida from the potential harms of artificial intelligence applications," he wrote on X in March. "It is especially important that we protect the most vulnerable among us: our children."

Regarding data centers, DeSantis signed a bill earlier this year that would prevent residents from bearing the costs of hyperscale data centers through utility bills and give local governments more authority over where those facilities are built.

Georgia
Brian Kemp is the governor of Georgia.

Derek White/Getty Images for The Coca Cola Company

Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp (R) sees AI as an economic opportunity the state cannot afford to ignore.

He has backed the expansion of data centers and has positioned Georgia as a potential hub for the country's AI infrastructure, meeting directly with OpenAI and Georgia Power in July to discuss OpenAI's activity in the state, sites of interest, jobs, and investment commitments.

Much of his approach has focused on building the electricity and infrastructure needed to attract AI investment to the state.

Hawaii
Josh Green is the governor of Hawaii.
