items.title: IT Recruitment in the Age of Generative AI
items.summary: The work has changed. Our hiring process needs to catch up. Roberto Penco, PhD Introduction For roughly the last ten years, I have participated in hiring students and full-time employees at a large corporation. I was one of several people involved in hiring for my unit. The process changed over time, but its general shape will probably sound familiar. We needed someone for a role. I usually wrote most of the job advertisement, human resources (HR) published it, and people applied. I concentrated on their curricula vitae. Cover letters mattered less to me, although colleagues may have felt differently. I wanted to meet the person behind the application. Sometimes finding candidates was difficult. At other times, I might have twenty applications and shortlist five. Those are illustrative numbers, but the next steps were ordinary enough: send possible interview times, agree on a slot, and offer alternatives when necessary. Earlier interviews happened in person; around the pandemic in 2020, we moved online. Technical testing varied. Sometimes we interviewed first and tested afterwards. With more applicants, the test might come first. In some periods, we had no test at all. Before 2020, candidates might spend an hour at our office working through exercises we had devised, using pen and paper. Later we used online assessment platforms, including Codility and then TestDome. [1, 2] I found both useful and preferred TestDome during that period. Creating a test and inviting candidates by email was convenient. Pen and paper had one advantage: the candidate could not blame the autocomplete. The underlying assumption was straightforward: we were hiring people to develop software, and writing code was a substantial part of that work. Asking them to demonstrate it seemed reasonable. That assumption needs revisiting now. In agentic development, we have already moved beyond manually writing code as the default way to produce software. Yet an interview can still remove the tools people use at work and make unaided coding the central qualification. I would change that. Give candidates a real problem. Let them use the tools. Assess what they deliver, how they know it works, and how much time and money the complete process requires. Figure 1. I would assess the whole path from a problem to a verified result. A narrow test of manual code production can miss the work around it. Background The change has already happened At Rails World in September 2026, David Heinemeier Hansson, the creator of the Ruby on Rails web-development framework, described the change at his company, 37signals: “Writing code by hand at 37signals is now an exceptional state.” He also described having gone several months without writing code manually himself. [3] Then he asked the audience who still wrote substantial amounts of code by hand each week. Looking at the raised hands, he estimated about five (0.4%). His account of the company’s changed working practice is the more useful evidence for hiring: manual code writing had already ceased to be the normal way they developed software. [3] This is the change I mean. Recruitment should respond to a way of working that already exists. Waiting until every company has adopted it would leave the interview behind the job. I’ve said this to my developers several times this year: If you’re writing manual code, you’re probably doing something wrong. Over the last six months, treating this only as a future possibility has become increasingly detached from the work we can already delegate. In my earlier article, Agentic Engineering , I discussed the old ambition of programming through natural language and the growing importance of specifying intent, constraints, and verification. I will not repeat that whole history here. The question now is what that change means when we choose the next person to join a team. [4] An artificial intelligence (AI) agent can pursue a task through a sequence of actions, using tools and their results to decide what to do next. A harness is the surrounding software that gives the model access to those tools and manages its working context. Research on SWE-agent, a system for solving software issues, showed that the design of this interface affected the agent’s performance. The model and the environment through which it works need to be considered together. [5] For a candidate, that creates work worth examining: giving the agent the right context, setting useful constraints, recognizing a bad direction, and deciding when the result deserves acceptance. An agent can finish the code before anyone notices we asked it the wrong question. Figure 2. The agent acts through its harness, receives tool results, and tries again. I would assess the candidate who sets the goal, supplies context, and decides whether to accept the result or redirect the work. [5] A much older way of instructing computers I remember a visit from my aunt, Gordana Ugrin Šparac, and my uncle, Professor Dimitrije Ugrin Šparac. My uncle was a mathematics professor at the University of Zagreb’s Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Computing, known locally as FER, where I studied in the late 1990s and early 2000s. He also wrote a textbook on applied probability. My aunt was a mathematician too. She told me she’d finished university in 1960 and continued her studies later, eventually earning a doctorate. [6] During that visit, she told me she had programmed with punched cards during the 1960s, in Croatia, then part of Yugoslavia. As she explained it, that was the only way available to her to get her code into the computer. A program could be a stack of cards, each carrying a line of code, that had to pass through a card reader. [7] What stayed with me was how directly she had worked with an earlier form of computing. The way we express a program changes. The need to make the computer do something useful remains. Hiring criteria should follow the work as it changes, too. Figure 3. My aunt programmed through punched cards. The way we express a program changes; the purpose of making a computer do something useful remains. Related work There is an established name for assessing someone through a task resembling the job: a work sample . The United States Office of Personnel Management describes work samples and simulations as exercises reflecting actual job activities. Its guidance also makes a point especially relevant to student recruitment: assess capabilities expected on entry, rather than skills the employer intends to teach afterwards. [8] Selection research supports taking assessment design seriously. Sackett and colleagues’ reassessment of personnel-selection evidence revised several widely repeated validity estimates downwards and found structured interviews particularly useful. For me, that reinforces the importance of a consistent process and clear evidence of the abilities we want to assess. [9] The specific idea of letting applicants work with AI has also been proposed before. Aishwarya Babu’s 2025 paper, Redesigning Technical Interviews in an AI-Driven Development Landscape , proposes exercises involving AI-assisted prototyping, review of generated output, and recorded interaction in a common environment. That is close to the approach I am advocating. It is a proposal, however, rather than a study showing better subsequent hiring outcomes. [10] Developer-productivity research gives us reasons to measure the complete task. Cui and colleagues studied three randomized field experiments involving 4,867 developers. Their pooled estimate indicated more completed tasks among developers induced to use an AI coding assistant. The experiments concerned coding assistance and task output in those workplaces. [11] A different result came from a study by the organization Model Evaluation and Threat Research. In an early-2025 experiment involving sixteen experienced open-source developers and 246 tasks in familiar repositories, allowing AI tools increased completion time by 19 percent. [12] In February 2026, the same organization explained that selection effects and the difficulty of measuring newer workflows complicated its follow-up work. That update does not support carrying the earlier slowdown forward as a universal verdict on current agents. [13] Together, these findings strengthen the case for observing what happens on a relevant task. Access to AI alone tells an employer little about the quality or efficiency of a candidate’s work. Assessment platforms are already responding. TestDome recommends assessing both unaided domain knowledge and AI-related skills. Its concern is that a lucky prompt can hide weak understanding. [2] Codility describes tasks designed around AI-assisted engineering, while CodeSignal released agentic coding assessments in March 2026. These offerings establish that the assessment format is already changing. [1, 14] My disagreement is with making unaided code production the default gate. A candidate’s understanding still needs examination. I would examine it through the decisions, verification, and adaptation required by the job, with the same tools available throughout. Stop Testing Developers for Work We Have Already Replaced Start with a problem the team recognizes The exercise should begin with a practicing engineer describing a bounded piece of work. It could be a simplified version of a problem the team actually encounters, with representative data and a reproducible starting environment. Here is an example I would use, rather than an account of a test I have already run. Give the candidate a small equipment-booking service and an existing dataset. Ask them to prevent overlapping reservations, preserve valid bookings already in the system, and make availability queries behave correctly. Allow them to use an agent harness, documentation, and ordinary development tools. That task creates useful decisions. What counts as an overlap? Can one reservation end at exactly the moment another begins? What happens when two requests arrive together? Where should the rule be enforced? Is the data model suitable? A relational database may be an appropriate part of the solution, but remembering setup commands would tell me little about those decisions. A booking system that works until two people use it at once has a generous definition of ‘works’. I would want the candidate to clarify missing requirements, choose an approach, and produce a working change. Then I would examine the evidence. Demonstrating one successful booking is insufficient if two simultaneous requests can reserve the same equipment. Figure 4. Both requests can see availability before either saves. I would want a candidate to expose this failure and demonstrate that the repaired system cannot accept both conflicting reservations. This is a constructed example of the behavior I would assess. After the first result, I would introduce a small change or a failing case. Perhaps the booking rules now require time between reservations, or a concurrent request exposes a defect. The candidate keeps access to the same tools and explains how they investigate and adapt the solution. Figure 5. I would look beyond the first demonstration. A shared follow-up gives me evidence of how a candidate investigates, adapts, and checks the work. This illustrates my proposal; it is not a comparison of measured candidate results. The follow-up matters because a successful first output can conceal weak understanding. In a small observational study of novice programmers, Prather and colleagues found substantial differences in how students understood and directed AI-assisted work, even when they could complete the task. That gives me a reason to look beyond completion alone. [15] I would also give candidates room to concentrate. A randomized study by Behroozi and colleagues, involving 48 students, found worse performance in an observed, think-aloud whiteboard interview than in a private setting. The settings differed in more than one way, and the participants were students, so it cannot settle every interview-design question. It does give us reason to avoid confusing performance under continuous observation with the ability to solve the problem. [16] Let them work. Then review the important decisions together, using the task record and the same core questions for each candidate. Measure what it takes to reach an acceptable result Quality comes first. A solution that loses existing bookings or fails under ordinary concurrent use has not met the task, however quickly it was produced. Once the result meets the required standard, time and cost become meaningful. AI Agents That Matter , by Kapoor and colleagues, argues for evaluating agent performance alongside cost and shows why an accuracy score alone can be misleading. Applying that principle to a candidate’s workflow is my proposal, rather than a hiring method the paper tested. [17] I would organize the evidence around a few questions: Problem solving: Useful clarification, a workable plan, and a sensible response when the first approach fails. Use of the harness: Relevant context, appropriate tools, and productive use of feedback from the agent and environment. Technical judgment: Checks that address the actual risks, diagnosis of failures, and an explanation of consequential choices. Result quality: Correct behavior, preserved data, and a solution that can be changed without breaking its requirements. Time: Time to the accepted result, including failed attempts and repair, with waiting and evaluator help recorded where practical. Cost: Expenditure across the whole attempt, including retries, alongside any operating costs that matter to the task. These are dimensions to adapt to the role. I would not pretend that a universal set of weights or a magic passing score follows from them. Token use could be useful evidence, too. Tokens are the units in which language models process their inputs and outputs. But the fewest tokens do not automatically identify the best candidate. Different models and representations use them differently; prices, caching, retries, and supporting tools also affect the bill. A longer first attempt can be cheaper overall if it avoids repeated failure. Skipping verification makes the first invoice smaller and the second one more interesting. The meaningful comparison is the complete cost of reaching the required result. Separately, a solution may cost more to develop but less to operate. For a frequently used service, that tradeoff can be sensible. I would want the candidate to recognize it and explain the decision. Figure 6. I would count generation, checks, retries, and repairs until the work meets the acceptance criteria. The cost of running the accepted result is a separate part of the comparison. [17] Give reviewers something concrete to judge “Good problem solver” is an impression. “Noticed that simultaneous requests could bypass the booking check, reproduced the failure, and repaired it” is evidence. Reviewers should record what candidates demonstrated, what they demonstrated after a standard prompt, and what remained unaddressed. The same core follow-up questions help make comparisons consistent. Prompt length and confidence of delivery deserve little credit by themselves. Comparable access matters as well. I would provide a common starting environment, tool options, setup time, and an explicit budget. Candidates should not need a personally funded subscription to show that they can do the job. If different harnesses or models are allowed, record those choices and interpret the result under those conditions. This requires technical assessors. HR can organize the process and explain expectations, while engineering colleagues or qualified external assessors define the task and interpret the work. We should not expect a recruiter to discover a concurrency defect from a polished demonstration. HR already has enough scheduling conflicts without having to debug ours. Platforms can make the process easier by providing reproducible environments, execution checks, usage records, and a way to review the candidate’s consequential actions. Some relevant capabilities already exist. The opportunity is to make evidence of effective agent-assisted work easier for employers to interpret, including its failures and costs. What this means for the person applying For a job seeker, I would change the preparation accordingly. Practice taking a task from an incomplete requirement to a result you can defend. Keep a record of the decisions that mattered: a question that changed the implementation, a defect you found, a check that failed, and the evidence that justified accepting the final version. Learn to work with a harness, but understand the process well enough to explain it without relying on one product’s terminology. Be ready to change the requirement and continue. Be ready to say where the solution remains weak. That is also how I would present an AI-assisted project in an interview. The fact that an agent generated its code is part of how the work was done. The valuable evidence is what I specified, what I checked, what I corrected, and why the result was good enough for its purpose. Employers and applicants need the same change in emphasis. One side needs to ask for this evidence; the other needs the opportunity to show it. Discussion and limitations The language underneath may change as well There is another implication of agents writing code that I find interesting: how much of our programming environment was chosen to make the work manageable for humans? Readability and maintainability are important benefits of high-level languages and frameworks. If an agent produces the implementation, the tradeoff can change. We can ask whether the best target should be closer to what the machine executes: assembly, a symbolic notation for processor instructions, or machine code itself. I think of RollerCoaster Tycoon , which I played and enjoyed. Chris Sawyer’s own account says it was written in approximately 99 percent x86 assembly, with some C for interfaces to Windows and DirectX. I regard it as a remarkable piece of programming. It also reminds me how much attention to implementation can matter when working within hardware constraints. Its history alone does not establish that assembly always beats a good compiler. [18] There is research behind the broader direction. Meta’s LLM Compiler work trained large language models on compiler representations and assembly, using compiler-generated data for optimization-related tasks. This supports the idea of generating useful training material from existing compilation processes. Finding good optimization targets and checking them remained substantial parts of the work. [19] AlphaDev used reinforcement learning, which trains a system through rewards for its actions, to discover improvements to small sorting routines at the assembly level. [20] More recently, SuperCoder explored improving compiled assembly with language models. These are demonstrations of low-level optimization under particular evaluation conditions. They do not establish that an agent can translate any request directly into an optimal executable. [21] My interest is in extending that direction. If human-readable source is no longer the thing a person must produce, perhaps we should train and evaluate systems more directly against the behavior and resource use of the final executable. Direct machine-code generation is one possibility; agents working through compilers and intermediate representations are others. Compilers already translate source programs into lower-level representations and can emit machine code. [22] There are two different potential gains here. One is more efficient execution: less time, memory, or energy for the same useful result. The other is cheaper generation. A smaller executable does not automatically require fewer model tokens, and a short output can still involve many unsuccessful attempts. I have not found evidence establishing the general claim that direct binary generation costs fewer tokens than generating high-level source. Nor does removing human typing make every framework unnecessary or make C universally ideal. Libraries still supply behavior we need, and software still has to be diagnosed, integrated, and modified. Those tradeoffs deserve measurement. This research direction extends the argument about efficiency. Recruitment can already change while agents continue producing ordinary high-level code. Figure 7. The solid route shows familiar compiler representations. The cited work optimizes particular compiler or assembly tasks; the dashed route marks the broader question I want to explore: producing reliable, efficient executables directly from intent. [19, 20, 21, 22] Removing a syntax test does not remove engineering knowledge A candidate who cannot recognize a broken requirement, investigate an incorrect result, or explain a consequential tradeoff has a problem. Agent access does not erase that. The assessment I am proposing still examines data models, behavior, architecture, and failure modes where the role requires them. Reading code or investigating a low-level defect may be part of that work. A well-designed coding exercise can reveal reasoning and debugging ability. My objection is to making unaided implementation the deciding gate when the job is performed with agents. For a specialized role in which manual low-level implementation is a real requirement, assess that requirement. For a student role, scale the exercise to what a new hire should already know and provide appropriate support. Both decisions should follow from the job. There is also a limit to what I can claim for the proposed exercise. The research reviewed here does not establish that this exact design predicts employee performance better than conventional coding tests. Agent benchmarks, productivity experiments, and plausible interview proposals cannot supply that missing comparison. An employer can investigate it. Pilot a task with clear acceptance criteria. Check whether reviewers agree about the evidence. Then examine whether the assessment relates to later accepted work, rework, learning, and collaboration, accounting for the role and the tools available. A single successful exercise gives us evidence under particular conditions; its value as a hiring method needs to be examined over time. Figure 8. I can examine a working result, a repaired failure and a decision trail in one exercise. I still need evidence from later work to learn whether that assessment helps me hire well. That is a practical next step for a hiring process whose assumptions deserve the same scrutiny as the candidate’s solution. Conclusion I used coding tests because they reflected a substantial part of the work we expected people to do. Agentic development has already changed that work. I would change the assessment with it. For the next developer vacancy, start with a problem the team recognizes. Give candidates access to the tools they can use on the job. Examine their decisions, verify the result, change a requirement, and look at the time and cost of reaching an acceptable outcome. For the person applying, practice that whole process and bring evidence of your judgment. In agentic development, manual code production has already ceased to be the default. Our interviews should assess how well people develop software under those conditions. AI assisted with research, drafting, editing, and creating the figures for this article. That update does not support carrying the earlier slowdown forward as a universal verdict on current agents. [13]

Together, these findings strengthen the case for observing what happens on a relevant task. Access to AI alone tells an employer little about the quality or efficiency of a candidate’s work.

Assessment platforms are already responding. TestDome recommends assessing both unaided domain knowledge and AI-related skills. Its concern is that a lucky prompt can hide weak understanding. [2] Codility describes tasks designed around AI-assisted engineering, while CodeSignal released agentic coding assessments in March 2026. These offerings establish that the assessment format is already changing. [1, 14]

My disagreement is with making unaided code production the default gate. A candidate’s understanding still needs examination. I would examine it through the decisions, verification, and adaptation required by the job, with the same tools available throughout.

Stop Testing Developers for Work We Have Already ReplacedStart with a problem the team recognizes

The exercise should begin with a practicing engineer describing a bounded piece of work. It could be a simplified version of a problem the team actually encounters, with representative data and a reproducible starting environment.

Here is an example I would use, rather than an account of a test I have already run.

Give the candidate a small equipment-booking service and an existing dataset. Ask them to prevent overlapping reservations, preserve valid bookings already in the system, and make availability queries behave correctly. Allow them to use an agent harness, documentation, and ordinary development tools.

That task creates useful decisions. What counts as an overlap? Can one reservation end at exactly the moment another begins? What happens when two requests arrive together? Where should the rule be enforced? Is the data model suitable? A relational database may be an appropriate part of the solution, but remembering setup commands would tell me little about those decisions.

A booking system that works until two people use it at once has a generous definition of ‘works’.

I would want the candidate to clarify missing requirements, choose an approach, and produce a working change. Then I would examine the evidence. Demonstrating one successful booking is insufficient if two simultaneous requests can reserve the same equipment.

Figure 4. Both requests can see availability before either saves. I would want a candidate to expose this failure and demonstrate that the repaired system cannot accept both conflicting reservations. This is a constructed example of the behavior I would assess.

After the first result, I would introduce a small change or a failing case. Perhaps the booking rules now require time between reservations, or a concurrent request exposes a defect. The candidate keeps access to the same tools and explains how they investigate and adapt the solution.

Figure 5. I would look beyond the first demonstration. A shared follow-up gives me evidence of how a candidate investigates, adapts, and checks the work. This illustrates my proposal; it is not a comparison of measured candidate results.

The follow-up matters because a successful first output can conceal weak understanding. In a small observational study of novice programmers, Prather and colleagues found substantial differences in how students understood and directed AI-assisted work, even when they could complete the task. That gives me a reason to look beyond completion alone. [15]

I would also give candidates room to concentrate. A randomized study by Behroozi and colleagues, involving 48 students, found worse performance in an observed, think-aloud whiteboard interview than in a private setting. The settings differed in more than one way, and the participants were students, so it cannot settle every interview-design question. It does give us reason to avoid confusing performance under continuous observation with the ability to solve the problem. [16]

Let them work. Then review the important decisions together, using the task record and the same core questions for each candidate.

Measure what it takes to reach an acceptable result

Quality comes first. A solution that loses existing bookings or fails under ordinary concurrent use has not met the task, however quickly it was produced.

Once the result meets the required standard, time and cost become meaningful. AI Agents That Matter, by Kapoor and colleagues, argues for evaluating agent performance alongside cost and shows why an accuracy score alone can be misleading. Applying that principle to a candidate’s workflow is my proposal, rather than a hiring method the paper tested. [17]

I would organize the evidence around a few questions:

  • Problem solving: Useful clarification, a workable plan, and a sensible response when the first approach fails.
  • Use of the harness: Relevant context, appropriate tools, and productive use of feedback from the agent and environment.
  • Technical judgment: Checks that address the actual risks, diagnosis of failures, and an explanation of consequential choices.
  • Result quality: Correct behavior, preserved data, and a solution that can be changed without breaking its requirements.
  • Time: Time to the accepted result, including failed attempts and repair, with waiting and evaluator help recorded where practical.
  • Cost: Expenditure across the whole attempt, including retries, alongside any operating costs that matter to the task.

These are dimensions to adapt to the role. I would not pretend that a universal set of weights or a magic passing score follows from them.

Token use could be useful evidence, too. Tokens are the units in which language models process their inputs and outputs. But the fewest tokens do not automatically identify the best candidate. Different models and representations use them differently; prices, caching, retries, and supporting tools also affect the bill. A longer first attempt can be cheaper overall if it avoids repeated failure.

Skipping verification makes the first invoice smaller and the second one more interesting.

The meaningful comparison is the complete cost of reaching the required result. Separately, a solution may cost more to develop but less to operate. For a frequently used service, that tradeoff can be sensible. I would want the candidate to recognize it and explain the decision.

Figure 6. I would count generation, checks, retries, and repairs until the work meets the acceptance criteria. The cost of running the accepted result is a separate part of the comparison. [17]Give reviewers something concrete to judge

“Good problem solver” is an impression. “Noticed that simultaneous requests could bypass the booking check, reproduced the failure, and repaired it” is evidence.

Reviewers should record what candidates demonstrated, what they demonstrated after a standard prompt, and what remained unaddressed. The same core follow-up questions help make comparisons consistent. Prompt length and confidence of delivery deserve little credit by themselves.

Comparable access matters as well. I would provide a common starting environment, tool options, setup time, and an explicit budget. Candidates should not need a personally funded subscription to show that they can do the job. If different harnesses or models are allowed, record those choices and interpret the result under those conditions.

This requires technical assessors. HR can organize the process and explain expectations, while engineering colleagues or qualified external assessors define the task and interpret the work. We should not expect a recruiter to discover a concurrency defect from a polished demonstration.

HR already has enough scheduling conflicts without having to debug ours.

Platforms can make the process easier by providing reproducible environments, execution checks, usage records, and a way to review the candidate’s consequential actions. Some relevant capabilities already exist. The opportunity is to make evidence of effective agent-assisted work easier for employers to interpret, including its failures and costs.

What this means for the person applying

For a job seeker, I would change the preparation accordingly. Practice taking a task from an incomplete requirement to a result you can defend. Keep a record of the decisions that mattered: a question that changed the implementation, a defect you found, a check that failed, and the evidence that justified accepting the final version.

Learn to work with a harness, but understand the process well enough to explain it without relying on one product’s terminology. Be ready to change the requirement and continue. Be ready to say where the solution remains weak.

That is also how I would present an AI-assisted project in an interview. The fact that an agent generated its code is part of how the work was done. The valuable evidence is what I specified, what I checked, what I corrected, and why the result was good enough for its purpose.

Employers and applicants need the same change in emphasis. One side needs to ask for this evidence; the other needs the opportunity to show it.

Discussion and limitationsThe language underneath may change as well

There is another implication of agents writing code that I find interesting: how much of our programming environment was chosen to make the work manageable for humans?

Readability and maintainability are important benefits of high-level languages and frameworks. If an agent produces the implementation, the tradeoff can change. We can ask whether the best target should be closer to what the machine executes: assembly, a symbolic notation for processor instructions, or machine code itself.

I think of RollerCoaster Tycoon, which I played and enjoyed. Chris Sawyer’s own account says it was written in approximately 99 percent x86 assembly, with some C for interfaces to Windows and DirectX. I regard it as a remarkable piece of programming. It also reminds me how much attention to implementation can matter when working within hardware constraints. Its history alone does not establish that assembly always beats a good compiler. [18]

There is research behind the broader direction. Meta’s LLM Compiler work trained large language models on compiler representations and assembly, using compiler-generated data for optimization-related tasks. This supports the idea of generating useful training material from existing compilation processes. Finding good optimization targets and checking them remained substantial parts of the work. [19]

AlphaDev used reinforcement learning, which trains a system through rewards for its actions, to discover improvements to small sorting routines at the assembly level. [20] More recently, SuperCoder explored improving compiled assembly with language models. These are demonstrations of low-level optimization under particular evaluation conditions. They do not establish that an agent can translate any request directly into an optimal executable. [21]

My interest is in extending that direction. If human-readable source is no longer the thing a person must produce, perhaps we should train and evaluate systems more directly against the behavior and resource use of the final executable. Direct machine-code generation is one possibility; agents working through compilers and intermediate representations are others. Compilers already translate source programs into lower-level representations and can emit machine code. [22]

There are two different potential gains here. One is more efficient execution: less time, memory, or energy for the same useful result. The other is cheaper generation. A smaller executable does not automatically require fewer model tokens, and a short output can still involve many unsuccessful attempts. I have not found evidence establishing the general claim that direct binary generation costs fewer tokens than generating high-level source.

Nor does removing human typing make every framework unnecessary or make C universally ideal. Libraries still supply behavior we need, and software still has to be diagnosed, integrated, and modified. Those tradeoffs deserve measurement.

This research direction extends the argument about efficiency. Recruitment can already change while agents continue producing ordinary high-level code.

Figure 7. The solid route shows familiar compiler representations. The cited work optimizes particular compiler or assembly tasks; the dashed route marks the broader question I want to explore: producing reliable, efficient executables directly from intent. [19, 20, 21, 22]Removing a syntax test does not remove engineering knowledge

A candidate who cannot recognize a broken requirement, investigate an incorrect result, or explain a consequential tradeoff has a problem. Agent access does not erase that.

The assessment I am proposing still examines data models, behavior, architecture, and failure modes where the role requires them. Reading code or investigating a low-level defect may be part of that work. A well-designed coding exercise can reveal reasoning and debugging ability. My objection is to making unaided implementation the deciding gate when the job is performed with agents.

For a specialized role in which manual low-level implementation is a real requirement, assess that requirement. For a student role, scale the exercise to what a new hire should already know and provide appropriate support. Both decisions should follow from the job.

There is also a limit to what I can claim for the proposed exercise. The research reviewed here does not establish that this exact design predicts employee performance better than conventional coding tests. Agent benchmarks, productivity experiments, and plausible interview proposals cannot supply that missing comparison.

An employer can investigate it. Pilot a task with clear acceptance criteria. Check whether reviewers agree about the evidence. Then examine whether the assessment relates to later accepted work, rework, learning, and collaboration, accounting for the role and the tools available. A single successful exercise gives us evidence under particular conditions; its value as a hiring method needs to be examined over time.

Figure 8. I can examine a working result, a repaired failure and a decision trail in one exercise. I still need evidence from later work to learn whether that assessment helps me hire well.

That is a practical next step for a hiring process whose assumptions deserve the same scrutiny as the candidate’s solution.

Conclusion

I used coding tests because they reflected a substantial part of the work we expected people to do. Agentic development has already changed that work. I would change the assessment with it.

For the next developer vacancy, start with a problem the team recognizes. Give candidates access to the tools they can use on the job. Examine their decisions, verify the result, change a requirement, and look at the time and cost of reaching an acceptable outcome.

For the person applying, practice that whole process and bring evidence of your judgment.

In agentic development, manual code production has already ceased to be the default. Our interviews should assess how well people develop software under those conditions.
